speakeroldname: Hon. Robert H. Winters (Minister of Public Works):
speechtext:
I beg leave to table a report, prepared at the request of my colleague the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) on the removal of Ripple Rock, which is a submerged navigational hazard in Seymour narrows, about 100 miles north of Vancouver. This report has been prepared by the associate committee for navigational facilities on the west coast, established by the national research council to study this project.
This committee was established after two previous attempts to remove the rock by surface methods, using techniques then known, were unsuccessful. This report concludes that the rock can be successfully removed either by surface operations, using present-day techniques, or by tunnelling. It recommends in favour of the latter as being the more positive approach.
I have asked Mr. Victor Dolmage, an eminent consulting geologist, who has had wide experience on the Kitimat project and other undertakings of this general nature, to indicate whether, in his opinion, this report could be translated into an engineering approach to the problem complete with plans and specifications.
Mr. Dolmage has now reported that in his opinion this is entirely practical, and he has been retained to prepare the required plans and specifications. It is anticipated that tenders will be called and that the work will be done under Mr. Dolmage's general supervision, on behalf of the Department of Public Works.
It is estimated that it will require some six months to prepare plans and specifications and that the rock can be removed within a space of two years after the contract is awarded. It is estimated that the total cost
involved will be in the vicinity of $2-5 million. Funds will be sought in the supplementary estimates for the next fiscal year in an appropriate amount to cover expenditures incurred in 1955-56.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask a question of the Minister of Public Works arising out of his statement. Can the minister give assurance to the house that the government will take all necessary steps to protect the residents in the vicinity of Ripple Rock against any possible loss or damage to property arising out of the blasting of the rock.
I can say that is one of the factors that have been taken into consideration.

Mr. Speaker, it is not our purpose to deal at length with this bill because, as was stated when the resolution was discussed, the bill is pretty much in line with that resolution. However, there are one or two things I would like to say.
I would refer first to a technical matter. I notice that in deleting subsection 1 of section 93 no provision has been made for renumbering the other sections. I believe that will have to be accounted for in some way. We now have subsection 2 as the first subsection in section 93, and no mention is made in the bill of renumbering the sections.
Then with regard to the table of rates, as I said the other day members in the official opposition as well as other members in the house have spoken at different times with respect to adjusting the rates of supplementary benefits since the rates of regular benefits were raised. I cannot help wondering just how the department got around the fact that despite subsection 1, which is now to be repealed, and which says that the rates of supplementary benefit shall be 80 per cent, during the period of time since the regular rates of benefit have been raised the rates of supplementary benefit have not been anything like 80 per cent.
As a matter of fact in some cases, notably in the lower rates, they ran about 80 per cent; but the higher the rate of daily contribution ran, the lower proportionately has been the rate of supplementary benefit which was paid. In the top class, for a person with dependents the amount paid was just 70 per cent, despite the fact that the act says the supplementary benefits shall be 80 per cent. I also note that apparently those persons
Unemployment Insurance Act without dependents have fared much better, in ratio, than those who had dependents; because even in the top bracket they managed to get 75-44 per cent whereas persons with dependents received only 70 per cent.
Probably the minister will explain that when he speaks. Now that the act is to be amended I mention this only as a matter of interest, but it has been a fact that people have been deprived of their just rights under this section.
Then with regard to section 94, last year when the season was well advanced we asked on two or three different occasions whether any plans were made, because of the urgency of the situation, to extend the period for the payment of supplementary benefits beyond April 15. The answer we received was that the matter was under consideration and, finally, that no action would be taken.
And so, Mr. Speaker, to support the remarks which were made in the house during the course of the debate on the resolution the other day, and at other times, and in order to bring this matter to a head I should move an amendment to clause 2. Shall I move it now or wait until the section is before the committee? Perhaps I should wait, and when clause 2 is before the committee of the whole I shall offer my amendment.
With those remarks, we are satisfied.

Mr. Speaker, there is not much one needs to say with regard to this bill more than was said when the resolution was before the committee of the whole house a few days ago. But I wish to emphasize by just how much this measure, useful though it may be, fails to meet the unemployment situation, at least in my part of the country. Before leaving home to come to Ottawa for this session I had more calls in regard to unemployment than at any time, I believe, since the winter of 1938-39.
I appreciate the value of this so far as it goes. The labour organizations have been asking for it for a long time. The bill does two things. It extends the period in which supplementary benefits may be paid, and it raises the amount of the supplementary payments to that of the regular payments under the Unemployment Insurance Act.
I was again interested in seeing the benefits under the Unemployment Insurance Act, which will now be the supplementary benefits as well as the regular ones, and noting the very little difference between the weekly benefits of a person without a dependent in the first category, who has contributed, and a person with a dependent. Under the act an unmarried person without a dependent now

Unemployment Insurance Act receives a weekly benefit, whether regular or supplementary, of $4.20. If he is a married man and has a wife and, say, one child he gets weekly benefits of $4.80, which is 60 cents more than he would receive if he were a single person. Then the amounts go up a little bit but, if we take the next category, it is $6 for the person without a dependent and $7.50 for a person with dependents.
What is required here is the raising of the amount of the benefit in all categories. I believe for some time at least these amounts could be raised without any change in the contribution. Because of the increases in the cost of living since the rates were established, those rates now provided are no longer adequate. The more unemployed we have, and the longer the period during which people are unemployed, the more inadequate the rates will become.
While there is no intention on our part to delay this measure in any way-as a matter of fact we wish to hurry it along as much as possible-we wish to say that as far as we are concerned it is very definitely an instalment, and a very small instalment, of what must be done for the unemployed if we are to enable them to live as citizens of this wealthy country should live.

It is not
my intention to hold up this bill at all. We all had a chance the other day to say what we had to say with respect to the general principle of the bill, and everyone agreed that action should be taken immediately.
When I was speaking the other day, I said in a general way that this was not going to be a cure-all for the problem of unemployment. I recalled vividly the situation that exists in my own constituency and in Drum-heller, where the coal mining industry is practically a thing of the past. In fact it got to be so bad that the provincial government had to allot, I think it was, $100,000 in order to move the miners out of that district entirely, because they could see that the coal mining industry, as far as western Canada is concerned, is getting worse rather than better.
Of course part of the blame can be laid on this government because of their policy in regard to the importation of foreign coal. But as I see it, the benefits from unemployment insurance are certainly not going to help in the Drumheller district. That is what I am concerned about. What are we going to do with these people after this legislation is in force and they have exhausted their 60-day minimum payments? That is the question that is bothering the working people of the day.
[Mr. Maclnnis.l

This is going to be of assistance. It introduces an increase in the amount of supplementary benefits, and it also introduces a new principle, in that we are now going to establish a 60-day minimum period during which supplementary benefits may be received. That is all to the good, but it is not in any way going to solve the problem of unemployment. I know that the minister will say right away that it was never intended to solve the problem of unemployment. But if things are going to continue to get worse, as they have in the past-and we must acknowledge that; I think the minister himself acknowledges that now-in the employment field, then what is going to happen after the supplementary payments have been exhausted?
This is only a palliative, and it is a mighty small one at that. It is going to be gratefully received; it is something the workers are entitled to. Hon. members and the minister should be greatly concerned; and he should bring down amendments, which he has already indicated he intends to do, that will materially assist in meeting the unemployment problem until such time as the workers are re-employed, not until such time as the 60-day period has elapsed. That is the responsibility of this government, and that is something we have to do.
Any further remarks I have to make, Mr. Speaker, I shall make when we come to the sections of the bill.

Mr. Speaker, the measure introduced by the government is highly satisfactory to me and I wish to say how much I am gratified by it. In the first place it is not to be denied that extra winter benefits have been and continue to be of very great value to workers faced with seasonal unemployment. The government must be commended for their decision in making these benefits equal to ordinary benefits.
The people of my constituency are kept very busy during the summer months in the building trade and other related fields. But during the winter they have more difficulty in finding employment of a permanent nature. I support this measure without any reservation whatsoever.
I understand, of course, that it is not calculated to strike directly at the unemployment situation in our area, a situation which at times, during 1954, has been a source of very real concern, to say the least. A number of industries in my constituency have had to face competition from foreign products. Goods manufactured abroad where labour is paid at ridiculously low rates have been flooding

this country, selling at prices which our own businessmen are unable to match since they have to keep on paying salaries designed to maintain the high standard of living of which we are so proud. That is why the government should be careful in advocating certain types of trade, even though trade may be generally advisable and even necessary to our national economy. They must do everything in their power to protect the interests of our own Canadian firms, such as the Dominion Rubber located in St. Jerome, or the Regent Knitting Mills of the same city, both of which are indispensable to local progress and employment. And if, through our trade policies, some plants or companies happen to be harder hit than others, the government must show them special consideration when it comes to letting contracts; such action will be appreciated by all.
Canada must trade with all the countries in the world and this trade, which is bound to be bilateral, is not without causing some unfavourable or irksome reactions here and there, in various spheres of our national economy. It therefore behooves the government to compensate, in one way or another, the business enterprises which, with a view to ensuring the progress of the community, make more personal sacrifices than others.
Along with the government I believe that Canada is going through a transition period and I hope to witness in 1955 the levelling-off of a situation which at times, in the last few months, has caused great concern to the people. Some of our bank presidents, in their annual speeches, remain optimistic about the future. According to yesterday's papers, the president of the Banque Canadien-ne Nationale, Mr. Charles St. Pierre, in his address to the directors on the occasion of the 80th annual meeting, made the following statement which is worth quoting:
The levelling off which was experienced last year was not unexpected. It is easy to realize that Canada cannot advance by leaps and bounds indefinitely without interruption. Periods of readjustment are indispensable to assure a sound economic development. The year 1954 was one of those stabilization periods. When it is looked at in its proper perspective, it will doubtless appear as a milestone in the expansion of our country.
Canada is a new country, a country in full growth, and, however great are its riches and however brilliant its future, it cannot escape the impact of the world's economic fluctuations. All the less so because, being a great exporting country, its prosperity is linked up with foreign markets. The business trend in the United States, the slowing down of which has had repercussions on our own economy, has again improved during the last months of the year. There is therefore reason to believe that our trade with our chief market will recover the lost ground.
However, Canada must also reckon with the other countries. Now the development of production in the world as a whole and the resumption of inter-50433-10
Unemployment Insurance Act national competition resulting therefrom indicate that the post-war period is at an end. Already there are signs that the return to a more normal order of things is giving rise to problems which demand efforts at readaptation. The necessary readjustments which have already begun will have to be pursued in several fields, and we are justified in hoping that they will be successfully achieved in the near future.
If a survey of the present situation may incline one to be prudent, none the less a sober optimism is justified at the beginning of this new year.
I have faith in my country, with its boundless resources and its promising future; it is far from having attained the maximum development. And the responsibility of this government, the duty of this parliament is to find the best way to make our Canadian homes safe from unemployment and insecurity.
The government intends to bring down more elaborate amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act. Personally I would have preferred the supplementary benefits to be paid from December 15 to April 1, instead of from January 1 to April 15. If the supplementary benefits were paid in December those entitled to them would get them during the Christmas season. That, to my mind, would make the act more humane still at a time when, for a lot of people, the end of the year is not so much a halt as a hope of better days.
And I have another suggestion to put before the government. I think the Unemployment Insurance Act could be amended so that the women who get married may recover the amount they have paid into the unemployment insurance fund. Such amount could be paid to them in a lump sum upon proof of marriage; should they seek employment later on, they would have to qualify again in order to be entitled to the benefits.
My county has three unemployment insurance offices. I want to pay a tribute to the personnel of those offices, to the way they receive the public and help them. They perform a task which is often thankless and always ticklish. They serve their country, they are the distributors of the wealth of a community during the all too numerous periods of hardship, and they are also the administrators of a great act which, 15 years after it was put in our statutes, proves how farsighted was the party to which we are indebted for it. The Unemployment Insurance Act has proven indispensable. If ever health insurance is added to unemployment insurance, the two words most dreaded by those who have to toil and moil every day of their life, unemployment and sickness, will make way for security. Security means peace for those who strive.

Mr. Speaker, as has been said by earlier speakers, this bill does two things; it increases the rate of supplementary benefits and it increases the minimum number of days from 18 to 60. As the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mrs. Fairclough) has said, our party has no fault to find in regard to these details. For several years we have been urging the government to do this sort of thing, and we are now glad to see that they have made it a reality. However, the bill specifies that the supplementary benefits can be paid only during the period January 1 to April 15. I contend that these benefits should be paid during other periods as well, and that is what I want to speak about this afternoon.
This bill is designed to alleviate hardship which would otherwise be experienced by people whose unemployment insurance credits have expired during the winter months. The government has learned at long last, after it has been pointed out to it during the past two or three years by the opposition, that people cannot live on 80 per cent of their unemployment insurance benefits. We are very glad to see that they have learned at last that-
They cannot live even on 100 per cent.

As the hon. member for Hamilton West says, they cannot live on even 100 per cent. I think that is so true. In refusing to pay these supplementary benefits until January 1, the government is assuming that people whose credits have expired before that date can in some miraculous fashion go into hibernation until the first of the year, and that they and their families are not going to require food, clothing and shelter until that time.
If it is necessary, and it most certainly is necessary, to increase these supplementary benefits from 80 per cent to 100 per cent of the regular benefits, then how much more necessary it is to increase the supplementary benefits from zero to 100 per cent during the months, say, of October, November and December! Hunger and hardship just do not understand this government's timetable. You can be just as cold, just as hungry and just as sick during the month of November as you can in the month of February.
If a man or woman is willing and anxious to work, and through no fault of his or her own cannot find work during the months preceding the first of the year, then somebody


must assume responsibility for that person and his family. The municipalities have no funds to do it; the provinces have no funds to do it. For some years past it has been the overwhelming opinion of all people who have made studies of this problem that this is a federal responsibility. They have urged the federal government to assume its responsibility in this matter. However, despite this overwhelming body of opinion, this government has continued to duck its responsibility, and I believe that by so doing it is showing a shocking lack of concern for the people for whom it has a primary responsibility.
This matter must be faced up to, and I think the time is long overdue for the government to come to grips with the problem and tell the Canadian people what it is going to do. For two or three years past I have asked the minister to tell the country what his views are on this problem, and the minister on behalf of the government has refused. I am going to ask him again today. I hope he will give us an answer, because the country is waiting for that answer.
I would like to cite a few opinions expressed on this matter by bodies set up by the government. First of all we have the Sirois report, which contains these two major points:
(a)	Responsibility for all unemployed employables rests with the federal government;
(b)	Responsibility for all other persons requiring public assistance rests with the provincial and municipal governments.
On page 42 of book II of the recommendations, the report states:
Unemployment relief should be a dominion function and provincial responsibility for other welfare services should continue . . .
As I stated on Tuesday, the late Prime Minister Mackenzie King, at the dominion-provincial conference of 1941, expressed his opinion forcibly, and because they are short I will repeat his remarks today because I think they are vitally important. They may be found at page 12 of the report:
The transfer to the federal government of the whole cost of relief for the employable unemployed and their dependents is the logical outcome of the experience of the past. It would prevent a repetition of the confusion, the inefficiency, the waste, the delay and the inequalities that have admittedly prevailed in relief since 1930 . . .
Another important opinion on this problem may be found at page 49 of the Marsh report prepared in 1943 at the request of this government. The report has this to say:
The logical location for the service ... is the dominion employment service, or some branch of it. The service that the local offices-

That is the offices of the unemployment insurance commission.
-would have to perform would be:
(1)	To register those applying for unemployment assistance.
(2)	To decide . . . whether a person should receive assistance; in what amounts; and for how long a period; and,
(3)	To issue the cheques or vouchers.
At the dominion-provincial conference of 1945, convened by this government, the following proposals were put forward by the government, and are found at pages 42 and 43:
As a part of the general arrangement with the provincial governments, the dominion government now proposes to establish a practicable and comprehensive system of assistance to able-bodied unemployed persons as soon as possible, rather than waiting until the need for it actually arises.
I would emphasize, Mr. Speaker, that these views were expressed nine years ago. The report continues:
Such a plan must fit into and make the maximum use of the structure and machinery of the existing unemployment insurance system. It would not be sensible to set up a different system requiring a different kind of administrative machinery. The plan proposes acceptance of dominion responsibility for unemployed employables, and provincial and local responsibility for unemployables.
Those were the suggestions put forward by the present government, and we are still waiting for their implementation. I would like to cite one more opinion, namely that expressed by the association of Canadian mayors and reeves. This important body meets annually, and on November 26 they submitted a brief to the dominion government in which they set forth the following:
The provision of financial assistance to a growing number of unemployed employable persons can constitute a severe drain on the fiscal resources of an urban community. Moreover, as the experience of the depression of the thirties indicates, an adequate program of unemployment assistance is beyond the capacity of a municipality to provide. In a federal country the responsibility for developing such a program must necessarily be assigned to the federal authority. Indeed, studies of this problem have consistently recommended that the federal government should assume responsibility for an adequate relief program for the employable unemployed.
This body comprises people who come in close contact with the problem of unemployment, and who look after the provision of funds to provide assistance. They are the ones who know most about it, and for years they have been urging the federal government to accept its responsibility, as in 1941 and in 1945 it agreed it would. The association of mayors and reeves is simply saying to this federal government, "Carry out the pledge you gave at two dominion-provincial conferences. You should accept your responsibility, and now is the time to do it".

The association has made its plea on four grounds: First, that the economy of the country is guided to a large extent by the fiscal policies of the federal government, and they in turn have an important bearing on employment as a whole. Second, they have pointed out that the municipalities simply do not have the sources of revenue necessary to meet the financial drain entailed. When this problem arises in a community it must be met. If the funds are not available it cannot be met. Third, the federal government is the only level of government capable of financing such a program. In this connection I would like to remind the house that the unemployment insurance fund amounts to nearly $1 billion and continues to grow each day. The fourth reason they have put forward is that the federal government is the only level of government which has the machinery necessary to administer such a program.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I think any logical and fair-minded person would agree that the reasons advanced by the mayors and reeves of this country are cogent and worthy of consideration. Their plea has been put forward on logical grounds, and I believe every hon. member, no matter in what part of the house he sits, would agree that something should be done to assist those who are suffering because of lack of funds with which to buy food and clothing. That can best be done by the government now accepting its responsibility. The acceptance of that responsibility is long overdue, and the government should now get on with the job.
Today at a later stage of the bill I am going to ask the minister once again if he will please tell this house what the attitude of this government is towards this problem. Do they agree with the opinions of the government in 1941 and 1945, or do they disagree? Let us have it one way or the other. Let us get down to cases. Let us know where we stand. Let us stop this shadow boxing, this shilly-shallying. Let us come out in the open and declare our hand. Let us get down to cases and try to solve this extremely important problem.

As I understand it-and I know the minister will correct me if I am wrong in this regard-when a plant is strike-bound and the strike is settled, some of the employees are not called back for days in some cases and for weeks in others. When these men apply for unemployment insurance, because of the fact that the plant has been strike-bound they find they

I wanted to ask the minister if there are in contemplation any changes that would take that situation into consideration. When he is closing the debate I would ask him if he would just comment on that matter.

It was a rather serious oversight for the people who are benefiting.

The fact that they did state 80 per cent did not mean that the intention was changed. As I said yesterday, it was the intention that there should not be any increase in the supplementary benefits until we had a chance to see the results of the 1952 amendment.
With regard to her remarks, which were referred to by a number of other members, as to the period over which the supplementary benefits extend, may I say that last year that matter was brought out clearly. I told the house that I was greatly concerned about it, as were other hon. members. We did not do anything about it at the time, but as the result of the serious situation last winter we carried out a careful investigation at the time and afterward. As will be

recalled, there were rather severe climatic conditions last spring, and work did not start very early. It will also be remembered that there were a large number in receipt of supplementary benefits in the middle of April when these formally ceased.
The unemployment insurance commission undertook and carried out a special survey of those who were drawing supplementary benefits in the week of April 15. They found that by the end of May more than half had either left the labour market or were working full time or part time, and that the proportions were something like this: working full or part time, 42 per cent of those who had been on supplementary benefits; retired or keeping house-the latter would apply mostly to women-15 per cent; and unemployed, 43 per cent.
That is a large percentage. But they took that 43 per cent, and they found that about 88 per cent of that 43 per cent had not kept alive their registration for work at the commission's local offices, and that only 3 per cent reported that they needed to get some outside assistance from other agencies. I am not at all understating the importance of that 3 per cent, but I am stating that by retaining the cut-off date at April 15 it is enabling us, under these amendments, to make that amount of money that will be spent effective in the cold, hard part of the winter rather than in the days when we always expect it to be warmer.
The hon. member for Kindersley referred to coal in his province.
The hon. member for Bow River.

I am not touching on the employment situation today. I shall defer that discussion, because it applies also to the eastern part of the country. With him and with the other members who have said it, I will admit that this bill is not a cure-all for unemployment in any sense of the word. As Minister of Labour I am charged by this house and by parliament with certain responsibilities. I will admit at once that the responsibilities I have the honour to carry out in the Department of Labour are mainly defensive rather than offensive, such as conciliation and trying to keep peace in the industrial family; and, in administering this act, to try to mop up where unemployment breaks out.
There will be an opportunity later to discuss this matter of unemployment. The hon. member for Broadview has made a speech on it, and I suppose he will make one on the speech from the throne, based on the lack of confidence motion of his party. But I say

that the bringing about of improvement with respect to this problem of unemployment- something which we all want so much-is not going to be effected by some minister waving a wand and passing one single piece of legislation. It is not going to be done in that way at all. It is going to be done by means of a great many things carried out conscientiously and effectively not only by this government but in relation to other levels of government. While the hon. member for Broadview quoted quite correctly the representations that were made to us by the association of municipalities, nevertheless I am sure he would be the first to admit that this government should not go over the head of the minister of municipal affairs in the province of Ontario-his own province-in order to do things in the municipalities without approval, co-operation and plans that should be worked out jointly between those two levels of government.
With regard to the comments made by my friend the hon. member for Terrebonne, may I say this. He also said that this bill was no cure-all and in turn expressed the wish that, instead of there being extension at the other end of the period, there be extension at this end, namely in the period before Christmas. In reality we do not get a great deal of abnormal seasonal unemployment before the Christmas holidays begin. While in some sections of the country it might be preferable to have more time at the beginning and perhaps less time at the end, on the whole we feel, from our experience up to the moment, that the present period is about right considering our limitations on money.
Is it not a fact that there was considerable unemployment this year in the lumbering industry, for instance, because of wet weather?

That is true, Mr. Chairman; there was. Again I say that was because of wet weather, and you cannot very well provide for that in a cross-country plan.
The hon. member also spoke about women in this connection. I hope that problem might be deferred until we come to the larger bill.
The hon. member for Middlesex East asked me to define more clearly the awarding of benefits in strike-bound plants. If it is not a matter that is of urgency today, rather than give an off the cuff definition of that I should like, because it is so delicate a subject, to give him a thoughtfully worked out memorandum on the question. It is something that is very important in his province now. I should be glad to do that.
The other day I promised the hon. member for Macleod that I would give the pertinent
Unemployment Insurance Act figures concerning the total supplementary benefits paid, and I think this will answer his purpose. From the fiscal year which ended March 31, 1950, to the fiscal year ended March 31, 1954, the total paid in supplementary benefits was $29,763,819.57. So that my hon. friend might have a point of comparison I will give alongside that the grand total of all benefits paid during that same period, from 1941 to 1954. The total, including the supplementary benefits, was $754,159,070.53. For the remaining period from April 1 to November 1, 1954, the total supplementary benefits paid amounted to $4,844,867.62, and the grand total of the regular benefits and supplementary benefits for that same period was $129,547,428.73. I hope that answers the question.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Does that mean that the fund has $30 million left out of that?

I was going to give the benefits paid out of that during the same period, which was $34,608,762, leaving a balance, if you look upon that as a special fund-we keep the records separately, but we do not keep it as a separate fund-of $24,847,272. Can the minister give the figures before we get to third reading?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Before the minister leaves these figures would he clear up one point that is bothering some of us down here? Then when I asked him for the amount paid in as a result of the one cent increase he said the figure was $59 million, out of which $34 million was paid. No.
This sounds like funny money.

Figures are very confusing when they are given in this way. I think perhaps we might ask the minister at some future date a very definite question in respect to these figures, or perhaps I could place it on the order paper.
When I spoke the other day I was particularly interested in the actuarial soundness of the fund, and what I really wanted was not merely the information as to how much had been paid into the fund and how much paid out of it. Rather I wanted comparative figures from year to year to discover whether or not, if there should be an extended period of unemployment, the fund would be depleted so that over a long period of years it would not be actuarially sound. The only indication we can get is by comparative figures from year to year.
I am not insisting upon getting the information at the moment. If it will help the minister I shall place a definite question on the order paper setting out what I want.

I thank the hon. member. And if he does not wish to put his question on the order paper, I am sure he will find those figures readily available when we come to the larger amendments. But I can assure him, as a member of the original committee, that the actuarial officials of the unemployment insurance branch have studied this matter in relation to the larger measure which is to come, with the intention of making sure that it is actuarially sound.
While I am getting the other figures sorted out I should like to refer to the question raised first, I believe, by the hon. member for Hamilton West, as to , the difference between the amount payable in supplementary benefits to single persons as compared with the amounts payable to workers with dependents, in the low wage categories. Our records indicate that 80 per cent of all the claims are in the class of $21 to $24, and that the rest are mostly unmarried persons. An effort will be made to make sure that it is relatively fair to all concerned, in working out the scale under the new legislation. And I think it will be understood that in the lowest scale of wages there are not very many workers with dependents.

Mr. Chairman, in answering me, the minister gave, I think, one of the most fantastic explanations I have heard, even for this government, when he tried to explain
*See correction of year on jmge 144, column 1.

why this government is ducking its responsibility with respect to looking after the unemployed employables in Ontario. He said that the government had some reticence about stepping on the toes of the Ontario minister of municipal affairs.
I want to assure him that there is nothing to be feared in that regard. The Frost government is very, very anxious for this government to assume its full responsibilities, as it said it would do in 1941 and 1945. So I would suggest to the minister that he climb out from behind that shield, because it is full of holes. I would advise him just to forget that explanation completely.
Now I would like to ask the minister if he would tell me plainly and simply what is the attitude of the government toward people whose unemployment insurance credits expired months prior to January 1. What is the government's attitude towards those people? Can the minister give me the government's answer?

As Minister of Labour my attitude toward them is to see to it that any of the facilities and the assistance we can provide is made available to them, and to see that the assistance given by this parliament is carried out, by way of finding jobs and making available to them any insurance to which they are entitled.

If your department, your unemployment insurance officers, cannot find that man or woman work, and he or she is anxious and willing to take work, and their unemployment insurance credits have expired, then what is this government going to do with regard to those people? Is it going to abandon them for those months until the 1st of January, or what is it going to do? That is a very simple question, and I would ask the minister on behalf of the government to give a simple answer.
I cannot accept the word "abandon" as it is used by my hon. friend. It is the wrong word entirely. We shall continue to do anything for which the federal government has authority.

Well, the federal government can extend the period, just as it is making a change now in the Unemployment Insurance Act. The federal government can extend this measure to include other months as well. I say you can become just as cold, just as hungry and just as sick in October, November and December as you can in January, February, March and the first two weeks in April. It is within the government's power to do something. Is the government willing to do it, or is it willing to abandon these people and expect them to go into some kind
Unemployment Insurance Act of hibernation where they can do without the necessary things of life? If not, what does the government expect them to do?
There is no use in the minister saying the government is doing everything it can. I say that everything you can do is not being done. You are trying to find them jobs, but you cannot find them jobs. A man finds himself without credits and without a job. He has a family and he has to eat, and so does his family. What are you going to do for him? I want to know that.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall the clause carry?
No. Then I assume, if the minister persists in remaining in his seat and not answering, that this government-
He answered.

He did not answer the last question. The Minister of Labour, by sitting and not answering, is giving tacit approval to the government being quite willing to see people go without the necessities of life during the months prior to January 1, because it is unwilling to take any steps to provide for them, as it agreed to do in 1941 and 1945.
The minister still sits there and says nothing. Therefore he is agreeing with what I am saying when I charge the government with being callous and cold, and with being far more interested in balance sheets than it is in human beings. All this talk about its great interest in human welfare is a lot of nonsense. There is no human welfare when there is not enough clothing and shelter, when you are out of work and have not enough to live on. This government is quite willing to allow people to continue in that state until some mysterious date-January 1-when, in its great wisdom, it says to all the unemployed to come out of hibernation. "Now you can come out; now you can warm up and start living again." Let us not have so much talk on platforms-
May I ask a question?

No question at all. You can make your speech after. Is this the same Liberal government which does things for the people and cares for the people? I say that, by the minister sitting there and being afraid to stand up and say on behalf of the government what it is going to do, it proves that it is not interested in human beings.

I do hope that when my hon. friend gets back from his third trip across Canada he will bring to this house a greater tolerance and a greater recognition of the fact that his fellow members also are concerned about the welfare of their fellow Canadians. He knows as well as I do that the

Unemployment Insurance Act question he has posed on this bill is an impossible one to answer at this time. I deny outright his statement that the minister, or this government, are not concerned about the welfare of their fellow Canadians. Furthermore, rather than have him stand in his place and direct generalities at this government or at the Minister of Labour, I would be much more impressed if he were prepared to place before me instances in his own city of men and women, unemployed employables, who are seeking unemployment relief this day, January 13, 1955.
He has made these statements here. I have been in my office ever since this house opened and not on one occasion, either by letter or personally, has he indicated to me that this problem in his province is greater than his province is able to meet.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order. Perhaps I should
indicate at this time that we are discussing clause 1 of a bill respecting supplementary benefits. I assure the hon. member for Broadview that I could not allow him to answer the questions which were posed by the Minister of Labour.

I rise because I think the
statement was out of order when the hon. member said the Minister of Labour was afraid to stand up, a man who has received the Victoria Cross. That statement should be taken back.

Mr. Chairman, I can now make myself an honest man with the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. It is nice to be able to blame mistakes on typographical errors, and in this case it is so on the sheet I have in my hand. When I said so carefully, "the 30th day of November, 1953", it should have been the 30th day of November, 1954. That makes it right.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall the clause carry?

Perhaps the discussion which has just taken place has carried us a little off the track. Since the hon. member for Broadview was permitted to continue with his remarks, I think he merited an answer from the minister. With that remark I am going to be satisfied. If the remarks were out of order, the Chair should have called him to order in the first place. We are all interested in that particular phase, and we can discuss it at great length when the other bill comes down to amend the Unemployment Insurance Act.
With regard to the amount of benefits paid, it would look very much as though my guess of Tuesday of this week at the resolution stage was pretty close, because I was merely taking the number of people who were insured and multiplying it by the contributions 

which I knew they must have made. I came to a surplus of $7,100,000, on the average, per year for the last four years. The minister's average is a little better than $6 million per year for the four years.
I am also interested in the statement that 80 per cent of the benefits paid were in the $21 to $24 a week class because this, in my opinion, leaves the government in a very peculiar position indeed in regard to the payment of those supplementary benefits. As I mentioned before, the act under which they are operating very clearly sets out 80 per cent, and the $21 to $24 a week class consists of the very persons who were not getting 80 per cent of the benefits at all but were getting 70 per cent.
With regard to the minister's other statement, I shall make some further remarks on clause 2. I wonder just where the department stands with regard to the poor administration of its own act over the last three or four years.

Before this clause passes I
should like to make a little correction, not of a typographical error in Hansard in the debate the other day but rather of an error I made. I said I was on the committee that originally brought in the bill. I said the bill was brought in before the war. I was trusting to my memory. I was speaking extemporaneously. The bill was brought in in 1940. The correction can be made now.
I should like to comment on one or two of the minister's remarks this afternoon. He indicated that in reality his responsibility was not to provide work for the people of Canada, and I agree with him. I do not think the minister's responsibility is to provide work at all. I do not believe it is actually even the government's responsibility to provide work, but it is the government's responsibility to so formulate policies as to keep industry producing at full capacity, no matter whether it is secondary industry or primary industry. If they are failing there, then they are failing in their over-all policy.
The minister recognizes that, because in another remark he made he said that in considering this whole matter there are a lot of things that must be conscientiously studied and made effective, or words to that effect. Yes, there are a lot of things; but I do want to say to the minister this one thing. While there may be a lot of things, nothing else will operate unless one thing is studied and made to operate effectively; and that is financial policy.
The Minister of Finance is sitting in his seat with his head on one hand as though he is deeply in thought.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Listening to the hon. member.

Without a proper financial policy of course everything else will fail. That financial policy should be one to keep industry working at full capacity; and when industry has produced goods for the welfare of the people of Canada, then it is the responsibility of government to see that that production is distributed to the people so they may receive the benefit of the work of their own hands.
So far as the government's responsibility to provide work is concerned, we have to do a lot of re-thinking on that. I believe the government is just as interested in this country as we are. I do not agree with the remarks made by the hon. member for Broadview a little while ago. Of course we have to excuse him. He has been out on the hustings, and he has got into the habit of talking that way. This is the House of Commons and he has to get over that habit when he is here. Of course we are all interested in human welfare; but we have to do a lot of re-thinking along this line.
The other day the Minister of Transport was asked a question by an hon. member with respect to whether or not the Canadian National Railways was doing anything to keep a certain number of men employed. I have forgotten the exact terms of the question, but the minister rose in his place and said the government was doing everything possible to keep those men employed.
That is where we have to do a little revision of our thinking. We must not assume that we have a railroad for the purpose of employing people. If that is the purpose of the railroad, then let us build a dozen more railroads or let the railroad run a dozen more trains. Whether or not there are passengers does not make any difference so long as it provides work. Railroads are operating to transport people and materials across the country. In the final analysis it is not necessarily a problem of providing work, it is a problem of getting the benefits of industry to the people after they have produced and done their job.
I read a statement the other day by a top ranking atomic energy scientist in the United States, who stated that if President Eisenhower gave the green light to a peacetime atomic energy program it would revolutionize everything overnight, and within five years we would perhaps have more unemployment than we have ever had as well as the greatest production we have ever had. The desert would blossom like the rose and there would be food aplenty for every living soul on the globe. We have to adjust our thinking and adjust our policy to a different age.

Clause agreed to.
Unemployment Insurance Act
On clause 2-Duration of supplementary benefit.

Under clause 2 we have for consideration the period during which the supplementary benefit would be paid. I am sure there are many hon. members of this house other than those on this side who would agree with the hon. member for Broadview, even though they are not outspoken in their agreement, that there are periods of the year other than the period January 1 to April 15 when people suffer because of the expiration of their benefit period. As far as the present season is concerned the period up to December 31 has passed, and we are now in a period during which the supplementary benefit would be paid. We hope that the bill dealing with a further revision of the act which the minister has said he will bring down will be before us before this session is much older, and for that reason I do not propose to word an amendment at this stage to include the period mentioned by the hon. member for Broadview. At the present time I think it would be quite sufficient to deal with the remainder of the current season; therefore I should like to make a few remarks in support of the amendment which I shall offer to extend that period.
Then a word with respect to the minister's figures of those who have benefited in the past. He said that as of April 15 last year it had been found that 42 per cent of those who had benefited by the supplementary benefits had secured work, either full or part time, and that some 15 per cent had retired. He admitted that 43 per cent of them were still unemployed and that 88 per cent of those 43 per cent had not kept their applications alive. I submit that the reason for that was that they lost heart.
Even if all that was left was 12 per cent I am sure that 12 per cent would be composed almost entirely of married men with families who needed every last cent that they could lay their hands on to keep their families alive. It does not matter to me what the volume is of those who would benefit under any extension; the fact that any portion of those insured and eligible for benefits should suffer hardship is quite sufficient. I feel that we cannot wait until spring is upon us to find out whether or not there is any need. Now that we are considering an amendment to this particular section I believe the matter should be settled at this tune at least for this season.
When April 15 comes along each year there is usually an entirely different outlook on the part of the department and even in the press as to the employment situation. Hon. members of this committee who have followed employment statistics year after year will recall

Unemployment Insurance Act that in late April, during May and even into June we begin to get reports that the employment situation is much better because there are fewer applications for benefits. Of course there are fewer applications for benefits after April 15, because those who have been receiving supplementary benefits find that there is no use applying for benefits. They are not going up to the employment offices more than once after April 15; when they have been told they are no longer eligible they just do not go any more.
The fact that they no longer apply is taken as an indication of increasing employment when very often it is nothing of the sort. Their benefits have run out; their supplementary benefits have run out, and because they are no longer eligible for benefits of any sort the news which goes out from the various offices across the country is interpreted by the Department of Labour as an indication of increasing employment. For all of these reasons I now move, seconded by the hon. member for Quebec West (Mr. Dufresne):
That clause 2 be amended by deleting the word "April" in line seven and substituting therefor the word "May".

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: After having read the hon. member's amendment, may I indicate some doubt as to whether it is in order, for reasons which I shall be glad to explain. However, if any hon. member has any observations to make on the question of whether or not this amendment is in order I shall be glad to hear him.
Mr. Chairman, I fail to understand what your reason is for considering this amendment to be out of order.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Hon. members will recall that the resolution which preceded this bill reads as follows:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Unemployment Insurance Act to raise the rates of supplementary benefit to the present rates of regular benefit and to provide a minimum of sixty days' supplementary benefit to those who qualify.
The bill is apparently a money bill based on that resolution. I would draw the attention of hon. members to May, fifteenth edition, page 678, where the following quotation will be found:
The guiding principle in determining the effect of an amendment upon the financial initiative of the crown is that the communication, to which the royal demand or recommendation is attached, must be treated as laying down once for all (unless withdrawn and replaced) not only the amount of a charge, but also its objects, purposes, conditions and qualifications. In relation to the standard thereby fixed, an amendment infringes the financial initiative of the crown, not only if it increases the amount, but also if it extends the objects and

purposes, or relaxes the conditions and qualifications, expressed in the communication by which the crown has demanded or recommended a charge.
I think this principle is well known to all hon. members, but perhaps I may also cite Beauchesne's third edition. Citation 486 reads as follows:
Reductions can be made in committee on the bill, but no grant can be increased except upon recommendation of the crown.
It seems to me that an amendment which substitutes the word "May" for the word "April" would increase benefits under the bill; would increase the financial obligations of the crown; and therefore would be out of order.
Mr. Chairman, I do not profess to be an expert on parliamentary procedure, but it seems to me that these are scarcely government funds. Contributions to these funds are made by workers and employers.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: And the government.
I might point out that 20 per cent is provided by the government. However, I rose because of two questions I left unanswered.
Dispose of the point.
He has.

In reply to the hon. member for Prince Albert I would state that the cost of administration for the unemployment insurance commission up to the year ending March 31, 1954, amounted to $26,096,722. I will carry out my promise to give the hon. member for Middlesex East a reply in full later, but in brief I would state that upon a general resumption of work any man not immediately called back will be paid benefits from the date of the reopening of the plant.

Mr. Chairman, now that the amendment moved by the hon. member for Hamilton West has been ruled out of order, I think we will probably have to approach the matter in another way if we wish to get something done.
I sometimes wonder if hon. members are as confused about the rules of order as they appear. I came into the house with the intention of making a speech almost identical to that made by the hon. member for Broadview, but I was afraid I would be stopped by Mr. Speaker; and having due regard for the propriety.of parliamentary procedure I refrained from making that kind of speech. I think probably the house and the country missed a very good speech.	.
Since it is not competent for a private member to introduce an amendment that would

involve the expenditure of money, that must not be taken to mean that it is against the rules of the house to urge the minister to introduce such an amendment, and quite frankly I see no reason why the minister cannot get one of his colleagues to move that the word "May" be inserted in this paragraph instead of "April".
There is no magic in the date of April 15 as far as the provision of work is concerned. The person who is unemployed on April 15 will very likely find himself still unemployed on April 16, and he has to eat on both days. Unless the government has some alternative means of providing persons referred to as employable unemployed with an income of at least as much as is provided under the Unemployment Insurance Act, it seems to me that this date should be extended.
All parts of the country are not in the same position with regard to the resumption of work disrupted by winter weather. Spring comes much later in some parts of the country than in others. By April 15, particularly in the southern part of my own province, there is a general resumption of work. But I was born in the maritimes, and work there may not commence until very much later. The advance in the season does not even permit the general resumption of agricultural work until later. Therefore persons in the maritime provinces, and this would apply also to a great part of Quebec, will be no better off as far as work is concerned on April 16 than they were on April 15.
I would suggest that the minister give consideration to this matter immediately, and introduce an amendment from April to May. I think it should be changed in any case so that every person who requires and has been receiving supplementary insurance can continue to do so for a minimum of 60 days. If such a person cannot find work, if there is no work for him, and if the government has no other method of providing for him, then his supplementary benefits should be extended until he has found work or for the 60-day period.

Mr. Chairman, I was not going to suggest any amendment to this legislation, but since an amendment has been proposed I find myself in full agreement with it. During my remarks a short time ago I pointed out that as soon as supplementary benefits expire the unemployed will find themselves in a very awkward position. The suggested amendment would go a long way toward relieving that situation by providing them with assistance over a longer period; and our group, I am certain, would support such a measure.
Unemployment Insurance Act

In reply to the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway I would say that searching consideration has already been given to his proposal. I would add that if we accepted his suggestion it would mean taking the funds from some other source. That is the long and short of it.
I am going to say this. It does not help the situation very much but it overcomes my hon. friend's question about what he is going to do on the 16th, the 17th and the 18th. In actual practice, of course, it turns out-and that is due to the unavoidable time lag, no matter how effective our local offices may be, in getting the payments out-that the worker whose supplementary benefits expire on April 15 is in receipt of payments fairly well to the end of that month. I should like to add just a brief word. I think anyone will admit that the Minister of Labour has taken an outstanding interest in the unemployed people in this country. Otherwise he would not have broken in on the debate on the speech from


the throne in order to put through this legislation. He might have been criticized for being in a hurry. My reason for rising was that I was hurt. I am not going to allow anybody to stand up in the House of Commons and say that the Minister of Labour is afraid to stand up and have his say. He is not afraid to do so.

To put the hon. member for Fort William at ease, let me say at once that I am not going to make any attacks on the Minister of Labour. But whether or not he is doing the best that can be done for the unemployed under the circumstances is something that cannot be settled just by the opinion of the hon. member for Fort William. It would be necessary to get the opinion of the unemployed on that matter, because they are the people who are hungry and cold.
It seems to me that when it comes to dealing with the unemployed-and I have felt this way for many years; I am not making an accusation against the Minister of Labour- we deal with the matter in a very uncivilized way. If there were as many people unemployed in April as there are in January or February, we would extend unemployment insurance in order to take care of them. The way we have looked after the unemployed in this country for years has always depended on how many were unemployed. If there were 10,000, 15,000, 20,000 or some number like that unemployed and hungry, they could starve. No one would take notice of them. But if we had 500,000 unemployed something would then be done about it, because it would be dangerous to have that many unemployed and going hungry. For our own safety we would do something for them. That is an unChristian and uncivilized way of dealing with a problem of this kind.
I suggest that we cannot think of the unemployed merely as a statistic, as I have heard them considered here in the House of Commons where it has been said, "Oh, yes; there are so many unemployed, but think of the number who are employed". The number who are employed are of no benefit to those who are unemployed unless they are getting something because others are employed.
Let us think of this question as it affects the individual and the family. When men are unemployed it does not mean that just those men alone are affected. It also means that wives and children are affected. Let us not be quite so smug about the matter and say that it is important to keep the fund sound. As the hon. member for Winnipeg North said, it is much easier to make sound a fund1 that has become unsound than it is

to make a family sound after it has become unsound through trials and tribulations beyond its ability to bear.
