speechtext:
It is an
agreeable duty, Mr. Speaker, to undertake some review of the speech from the throne and make certain comments on the problems laid squarely before the house by the amendments which have been introduced.
Realism is a desirable quality in a speech from the throne. If one is to judge by what this speech from the throne has to say about the nature of unemployment in Canada, it is a document hopelessly lacking in realism. We read this sentence in it:
Some unemployment of a regional and seasonal nature is being experienced.
What a monstrous understatement, Mr. Speaker! It is no wonder that what the speech from the throne proposes in the way of legislative and other remedies is very fragmentary and of the nature that it is, 

based upon an approach so hopelessly lacking in realism to a national problem. I should like to hear some hon. members opposite comment freely and candidly on that statement as applied to the unemployment situation in Canada. I should like to hear the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Croll), for example, make his comments upon it. I should like to hear some other hon. members in the house who sit opposite, who apparently are closer to the unemployment conditions than are those who wrote this speech from the throne. I should like to hear their comments upon a description of that kind.
There have been some remarks from the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) concerning the business of the house and the way it is to be transacted at this session. I am glad to see an indication that more of the government business is appearing on the order paper at this stage of the session, so much earlier than has been the practice in the past.
For my part, and I speak as an individual, I am glad to know from the Prime Minister's remarks that he has acceded to the suggestion I have made for some time that we should experiment with the appointment of a committee on estimates. I wish the Prime Minister would indicate what are the five or six departments whose estimates he proposes to have referred to that committee. It would be of assistance to us in this part of the house, and I think of interest to all members in the house, to know what those departments are to be. I would ask, for instance, whether the Department of National Defence is to be one of those departments. Is the Department of Defence Production one of the departments the estimates of which are to be referred to that committee on estimates?
I hope that at an early date steps will be taken to set up the special committee to review the activities and finances and the annual report of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. At the last session of parliament when this question was raised the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. McCann) indicated that the government would be favourable to the appointment of such a committee at this present session; and I hope steps will be taken to have that committee appointed and launched on its labours at an early date.
Something has been said about the length of the amendment introduced on behalf of the official opposition by the acting leader. We have no apology to make for the length of that amendment or for the number of problems we have found it our duty to lay before the house in the terms of the amendment.
What is the great variety of subjects raised there? There is the fact that our trade has

fallen, that the government has failed so badly in the marketing of our wheat surplus, that unemployment has grown to the point where it is a serious and urgent problem, that taxes are very high, that high costs are pricing many Canadian products out of the market, that waste and extravagance do exist in the government service and that the government has shown no willingness to grapple with them, that there is much need of greater processing of the natural resources of this country within Canada in order to provide more employment for Canadian workmen, and then there is the paragraph dealing with the provision of health and hospital services in Canada for those who need them.
Mr. Speaker, if the government had not neglected and ignored so many urgent Canadian problems it would not be necessary for us of the official opposition to introduce so lengthy an amendment in condemnation of the government for its failure to take resolute measures to cope with these problems. We have not catalogued all the government's failures in the amendment, but we have catalogued some of them. But these do offer basic considerations, and they are our conception of what is needed immediately by way of a government program. And to that extent they are an expression of our want of confidence in this government.
Sir, the first of the subjects dealt with in our amendment relates to trade. As we point out in the amendment, there has been a serious failure in that respect on the part of the government, and we express our regret that His Excellency's advisers-
-have failed to take or to recommend the necessary measures:
(a) to retain and expand Canada's markets abroad for our production, particularly of wheat and other products.
Canada's international transactions on current account resulted in the year 1953 in a deficit of $439 million, as compared with a surplus on current transactions in 1952 amounting to $164 million. The figures are not yet complete for 1954, but the deficit on current transactions for the first ten months of the calendar year 1954 was $330 million. This therefore is a serious problem, and must engage the attention of all hon. members.
In the first place, sir, there has been a serious decline in our commodity trade. Taking the first ten months of 1954-because the figures are complete only to October 31, 1954-our imports as compared with the same ten months in 1953 showed a reduction of 8 per cent. Our imports from the United States were down by 11 per cent, and from the United Kingdom 9 per cent.
Now let us look at the export figures. For those same ten months, as compared with
The Address-Mr. Fleming the corresponding ten months of 1953, our total Canadian exports showed a reduction of 8-2 per cent. Our exports to the United States were down 5-5 per cent, our exports to the United Kingdom were down 10 per cent and those to other countries of the commonwealth were down 20 per cent.
The main factor in the over-all decline in our exports has been the decrease in our exports of wheat, wheat flour and other grains. The decline in our trade is serious. The decline in these ten months followed a similar decline which has been going on now for some two years, and it is serious enough both in dollar figures and in volume figures to demand the attention of the government.
There is another serious factor in our trading position-and we do not raise it now for the first time. It is the extent to which our trading eggs have been disproportionately and dangerously placed in one basket. In these ten months of which we are speaking, namely the first ten months of 1954, our exports to the United States were 60-4 per cent of our total exports. And if you will look at the corresponding figures for the first ten months of 1953 you will find a similar situation. Indeed, looking at our total trade with the United States, both export and import, we will see that the proportion or percentage has remained constant. In the first ten months of 1953 and the first ten months of 1954, alike 67 per cent of our total trade, both import and export, was done with the United States.
Again we draw the attention of the government to this dangerous situation-not that we want to curtail exports to the United States, but we want to see much more energetic and aggressive measures used to expand our exports elsewhere. And, above all, we want the government to come to grips with the essence of the Canadian trade problem, which has been featured by a decline in Canadian trade with the United Kingdom.
Sir, this must be said about our trade with the United States, that our exports to that country are largely of Canadian raw materials, materials drawn from our soil, and which in very substantial measure are sent abroad to be processed in the United States. We in Canada should be seeking more effective methods of processing more of our raw materials at home. One of the best examples of what has been accomplished in that regard is to be found in the pulp and paper industry. Had it not been for the firm action of some provincial governments, notably that of Ontario, led by the Hon. George Drew, and others-and the province of Quebec is also a very good example-we would still be exporting our forest products in their original
152	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Fleming form. Cutting regulations of the provincial governments have assisted greatly in the development of this industry here at home, and it has provided needed employment for Canadians.
But, sir, lest any think that this pattern or picture of decline in Canadian trade is part of a world-wide pattern, let us take a corrective look at the figures. The figures I now give the house are figures of world trade drawn from international monetary fund publications. They are figures of total world trade, that is to say of the non-communist world. These figures have all been placed on a common basis and are expressed in United States dollars. Necessary adjustments are made in these statistics for purposes of reaching a common basis; and Canadian trade figures, like those of other countries, have been converted for that purpose. When I speak about quarterly statistics, it will be understood that these figures are designed to express the annual rate as the inference may be drawn from the quarterly figures.
What has been the trend in world trade in the last two years? Sir, these figures show unmistakably that the world trade trend has been upward in this period while Canadian trade has been going downward. In 1953 the total annual volume of world trade, both export and import, expressed in figures for the first quarter, amounted to $146 billion. The figure for the corresponding first quarter of 1954 was $148 billion, indicating an increase of $2 billion. In the second quarter of 1954 the increase was from the annual rate of $153 billion of world trade in the second quarter of 1953 to $158-7 billion. Unmistakably, Mr. Speaker, the volume and the dollar value of world trade have both been rising. Against that, Canada's figures show a decline.
Canada's percentage of the total of world trade is likewise declining. In 1953, Canada's percentage of the total world trade, both export and import, was 6 [DOT] 2 per cent. In the first half of 1954, which takes us to the last date for which figures are available, it has dropped to something like 5 * 5 per cent. It is a significant decrease, one that should command attention and concern.
But, sir, let us look further at the figures of British trade, and our trade with the United Kingdom. In his speech on Monday, even in its most soothing tones, there was a gloomy, an unmistakably gloomy, note in the Prime Minister's remarks when he came to the subject of our trade with the United Kingdom. It was indeed the gloomiest and most futile part of his entire speech. While Canada's trade has been going back, the trade


of the United Kingdom has been increasing. British exports in 1953-these are again expressed in terms of United States dollars- aggregated $7,525,000,000 United States dollars. The figures are not complete for 1954 but they indicate-those figures that were available up to the end of the third quarter of 1954-that British export trade will probably rise to $8 billion United States dollars, an increase over 1953 of about 7 per cent in value.
We are perhaps more concerned with British imports, especially our proportion of Britain's imports from abroad. In 1953, Britain's imports totalled $9,366,000,000 United States dollars. The figures are complete only to the end of the third quarter of 1954, but they indicate that we may expect they will aggregate about $9,500,000,000. There is an increase of something like 2 per cent in British imports in 1954 over 1953. But what about Canada's proportion of this increased British trade, this trade that we so badly need, this British market that has been our traditional market, our best market, our most stable and most dependable market, particularly for the large agricultural surpluses of this country? What do the figures show about our proportion of the British trade? Here is the proportion of British exports to Canada: In 1938, 4-4 per cent; in 1953, 6 per cent; in 1954, for the first eleven months, our proportion has dropped to 4-9 per cent. A very significant drop from the 6 per cent of 1953! But let us look then at the British imports from Canada. In 1938 British imports from Canada amounted to 8-6 per cent of British total imports. In 1953 they amounted to 9-1 per cent. In 1954, for the first eleven months, that had dropped to 7-8 per cent, a very serious decrease, Mr. Speaker.
I mentioned earlier that much of the drop in our trade, particularly export trade, has been traceable to the substantial reduction in our export of wheat, wheat flour and grain. Why has this special significance? The reasons are twofold, sir. In the first place, wheat is a government monopoly as to its marketing and export; but there is another reason. Wheat plays an almost unique part in the health and strength of the Canadian economy. What has been this country's record in the export of wheat? Well, for the crop year that ended on July 31, 1953, we exported a total of 385-5 million bushels. For the crop year ended July 31, 1954, that figure had dropped to 255 [DOT] 1 million bushels, a drop, sir, of 35 per cent. For the crop year ended July 31, 1953, our exports of wheat and wheat flour to the United Kingdom aggregated 122-9 million bushels. In the crop year ended July

31, 1954, that export total had dropped to 82 million bushels, a drop of one-third, sir, as compared with the previous year. Is it any wonder, sir, that we draw the attention of the house, with a very urgent degree of concern, to this lamentable drop in Canadian wheat exports?
If you look further, sir, at the drop in the income of the farmers of Canada and consider that farm income in Canada has now dropped to the lowest point in seven years, that for the past several years we have witnessed year by year a drop that has averaged about 11 or 12 per cent as compared with the previous year, you begin to have some appreciation of how serious is the problem confronting the basic element of agriculture in the Canadian economy.
What have we heard from the government? It was a pathetic thing we heard in the speech of the Prime Minister on Monday when, in relation to the export of Canadian wheat, he took comfort out of the fact that our proportion of British imports of wheat had dropped less than the United States but more than the Argentine and Australia. Well, sir, there are only four of these great wheat exporting countries. The other three countries are our competitors. The two that the Prime Minister concedes as having a better record than ours are not countries that have anything like the amount of wheat to export that we have. Why should Canada not be in first place in the proportion of the exports that are going to the United Kingdom market that Canadian exporters enjoyed? Why should we be satisfied with third place, in terms of holding our proportion, as the Prime Minister apparently is? Has the agricultural economy of this country not come to a pretty pass; has the marketing of wheat under the government's monopolistic control not come to a pretty pass in Canada when we have to depend upon adverse climatic conditions to contribute a solution to the problem of the Canadian wheat surplus that this government proved itself incapable of solving? The sigh of relief, the political sigh of relief, from the government opposite when the promising wheat crop of the west turned into a failure last summer could have been heard almost around the world.

speechtext:
We might at least have had a debate on the subject, but apparently we are not going to have, even during the course of this discursive debate on the address, any statement of the position the Prime Minister is going to take in London. During the course of his speech on Monday we heard on this subject nothing but words of amiable futility, remote unconcern and gloomy despondency.
We have not forgotten that when the Prime Minister returned from his commonwealth tour on March 18, 1954, a tour undertaken with the good wishes of all the parties in this house, a tour to which we had attached such high hopes, he did not during the course of his long report say one good word for that important institution, the British commonwealth of nations-not a word.
We in this part of the house think it is about time there was some indication from the government that it attaches not only political but economic importance to this institution, this commonwealth of nations. When Canada is represented at a conference of that kind, if Canada means to make that conference effective, Canada should exploit to the limit the importance of increased trade within the commonwealth.
While I am speaking of conferences I should like to renew the demand that this party has made times without number for a dominion-provincial conference. The need for such a conference is greater today than it was when this subject was last raised during the 1954 session. Since the last session some remarkable things have happened. Last September the Prime Minister girded on his armour and launched a carefully calculated and planned attack on the policies of Quebec. He succeeded in arousing feelings against his own province. It was no contribution to national unity that he made. But let us pass on.
Where is this issue today? Somehow or other on the field of battle, that field of the Prime Minister's choosing, there suddenly descended a lull. The Prime Minister called off the crusade, he broke off the engagement. There were some talks, but following the talks there has been again complete silence. There would have been no necessity or occasion for talks between the Prime Minister


of Canada and the premier of Quebec if the proper policy which we have advocated had been followed before, namely, the calling of a general dominion-provincial conference. This is something of concern to all Canada; it concerns all the provinces of Canada. It is not just an issue between Ottawa and Quebec. It is small wonder then that with this further conspiracy of silence the suspicions of the other provinces have been aroused.
What has happened? Why this silence? Mr. Duplessis has made it known that his proposals were placed in the hands of the federal government many weeks ago and apparently action has been awaited on the part of the government opposite. What are they waiting for? In the name of parliament we demand a report and we demand the calling of a dominion-provincial conference, the place where matters of this kind ought to be discussed.
We have asked in our amendment for some relief for the Canadian taxpayer from the heavy burden of taxation. We have asked for this in the name of the Canadian producer and in the name of the Canadian consumer. We are in an era of competition. Jobs of Canadians are at stake. The health of the Canadian economy is under assault. In the face of the kind of competition which Canadian producers are having to meet today the government must do more than preach the virtues of increasing our imports, as they are apparently content to do, judging from the speeches made during the course of this debate.
We should tell the government, and we should tell the C.C.F. as well, that exports are a good deal more than a mere by-product of imports. The Canadian producers, in facing the kind of competition they are confronted with now, must have material assistance in reducing their costs of production if they are going to meet this competition and continue to provide jobs for Canadian workmen.
This government, which is taking virtually half of the income of every Canadian corporation, which is levying heavy sales and excise taxes, must take this problem seriously and meet its responsibility by reducing this heavy load which is hampering the Canadian producer today and which is costing the jobs of Canadian workmen.
We have asked as well for an end of government waste and extravagance. We have asked that the government dedicate its efforts to increasing efficiency because that efficiency will create economy. But the government continues to be impervious to appeals of this kind. They turn a deaf ear

when appeals come from this side of the house for elimination of waste and extravagance and the reduction of taxation. They have thwarted persistently every effort that has been made in this house to inquire into the degree of efficiency in the government service with a view to improving it. Where reports have been made before on conditions in the government service, exposing inefficiency and other things there, the government has resorted to every stratagem and every resource to prevent the conditions disclosed in such reports from becoming known in this house and to the Canadian people.
It is true that one report did escape outside the government's iron curtain, the Currie report of two years ago, but we may be sure, and we have seen abundant evidence of this, that the government intends that no other fugitive shall escape outside that government iron curtain. Indeed they made the most strenuous and sedulous efforts to round up that fugitive and get him back behind the iron curtain after he escaped.
Throughout the government has shown the most blatant contempt for the institution of parliament. Upon the shoulders of every government supporter in this house rests the unhappy responsibility of bearing whatever part he has played in allowing the government to impose this iron curtain that has denied to parliament and to the Canadian people information that ought to have been laid before them. Yes, government supporters by their docility and submissiveness have assumed their share of the responsibility for what has happened.
When the government is preaching to Canadian producers that they must be efficient and competitive, and eliminate waste and extravagance, let them begin at home and start by cleaning their own house.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to bring the subject matter for the time being to something else not quite so exciting and perhaps not quite so controversial. I think that a great number of hon. members were as interested as was I when they saw in this morning's Montreal Gazette the report that perhaps a tax rental agreement had been arrived at between the government of Canada and the province of Quebec. I hope that is so. I hope it is so on a fair and equitable basis to all concerned. I should like to see every province within this agreement, believing as I do that when every province is in it, then Canada as a nation will be so much stronger.
We in the C.C.F. want to see this agreement and we hope it will be achieved on the fairest terms to all. We say again, as we have said in the past, that we insist without any qualification on the right of the people of Quebec to their constitutional rights as well as the unwritten ones which are accepted in civilized society, just as we on the other hand ask for reciprocity and insist that we also have rights. But there is this one thing that I must point out. There is one price that we will not pay for Quebec participation and that is the wrecking of the tax agreements. I do not know what the facts are. I do not know whether or not the report was accurate or inaccurate. I therefore intend to leave the situation at that point, hoping that an agreement has been arrived at and hoping that the agreement will be good for Canada. If that is so then certainly we welcome such an agreement.
I want to say a few words about the unemployment situation. The other night my colleague the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch), speaking in this debate, pointed out the masterly job which either the Liberal apologists or Liberal publicity men had achieved in selling the people of Canada the concept of the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) as "Uncle Louie", an appellation which indicates affection. It is perhaps arguable that the Canadian people have no great regard for a paternal society and that therefore their desire is all for an avuncular one. But the pity of it today is that this government, under the present avuncular society, is nevertheless making tens of thousands and hundreds of thousands of Canadians cry "uncle". I am talking about those Canadians today who, through no fault of their
The Address-Mr. A. Stewart own, are unemployed, who cannot get work and who want to work. This government is apparently doing nothing about the situation. Last year it was obvious, from looking at the treasury benches, that there was a degree of lethargy and apathy which I thought could not have been increased. But this year it is even worse, with one exception. The Minister of Transport (Mr. Marler) has not yet been contaminated with the lethargy which afflicts the rest of his colleagues and I hope for his sake that such a thing never happens.
I remember reading a description of a British government some years ago. It was described as a government of exhausted volcanoes. Nobody would suggest that this government was a government of exhausted volcanoes because there would be no excuse for such an exaggeration. To describe it as a government of exhausted molehills might be more accurate; and I am convinced that is what a great number of Canadians today think this government is. Not only is it apathetic and lethargic in the face of present social problems but it is self-satisfied. What is even worse, as we have been told by an excellent witness, it is incompetent. I am not advancing my own concept of incompetence. I call upon the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) who knows his colleagues much better than I do. Let me quote from page 40 of Hansard where my leader the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) read this extract from a speech of the Prime Minister:
"We have a country where there should be work for everybody and if we are not smart enough to organize the economy of the nation to provide work for everybody we are incompetent."
Manifestly the government is not smart enough to organize work for everybody. Therefore, by definition, the government is incompetent; and when the Prime Minister himself makes that assertion, who am I to disagree with him?
Not only have we unemployment today but it is increasing and it is going to get worse. There is no plan or project that we have seen except the blasting of Ripple Rock out of the water. What is that going to do from the point of view of unemployment? What help is being given to men whose lives are being squandered in idleness? That is the problem which faces this house and that is what this government must answer for because within a few months there are going to be over a million people close to relief. That is not to say that there will be a million people unemployed but many of
158	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. A. Stewart those who today are unemployed have dependents; they have wives and children and they are going to be close to relief unless the government takes action to help them.
I cannot altogether agree with the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gregg) when he regards his position in such a circumscribed way as he did this afternoon. I can perhaps agree that unemployment cannot be cured by legislation. However, unemployment can be greatly alleviated by sensible and reasonable fiscal policies which this government has not yet disclosed to us.
I see this situation in my own city of Winnipeg where we are dependent for our prosperity on the well-being of the farmers. When the farmer's income has been cut, as it has been this year, we in the city are going to suffer. If you cut down the farmer's income, you cut down what he spends in the city. And if you cut down what he spends in the city, you create unemployment or you create short-time employment and you have a demand for lower wages. Do that, and once again we are in the spiral of depression.
I might give the house a case in point. Before I left Winnipeg a couple of weeks ago I was talking to the bargaining committee of a union which has been conducting negotiations with a particular employer. The employer in Winnipeg took this stand: In your last contract your starting wage was $1.22 an hour. It is now going to be $1 and if you do not like it, I can get all the men I want for 85 cents. I do not think he could get all the men he wanted for 85 cents but he certainly could get some. I cite that instance in order to show the dangerous situation which is prevailing where employers are deliberately, as a matter of policy, cutting down purchasing power still further.
It is necessary that the government see that, as far as possible, purchasing power is restored in the widest possible way. But the government says: We have another method; when times get tough, we must go in for economizing. One of the aspects of economizing which they introduce is that teams are apparently sent through each department and a little clerk is hoofed out here and another little clerk is booted out there, and economizing is the word used for that procedure. But there is no economy. There is no economizing going on when there are almost 300,000 people unemployed and human resources are being wasted. It is to that aspect of economy that I should like to see this government devote its time. There is a loss in income which can never be


replaced. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) ought to have some appreciation for this argument because, with unemployment as it is now, there must be a loss in national income per week of at least $12 million, and within a few months' time it is going to be double that amount. Yet we have these hundreds of thousands unemployed, with little hope for them. What would the supporters of free enterprise in this house say if they saw capital being destroyed? I refer to capital either in the shape of finance or capital in the shape of things like machines, implements or buildings. They would be howling murder about it. Yet you are destroying the capital of men when you destroy the time they might be working. A man can never get back the hours which he has lost. A man can never regain the days he was unemployed; his capital is being destroyed.
There is another aspect to it. How are we going to approach this problem of the worker in industry and the owner of industry? Today, by and large, in corporate industry the owner is one who lends his money to industry. He can get that money back whenever he wants through the medium of the stock exchange. The owner lends his money, but the worker gives his life. Who then has the greater claim, morally or any other way, on the proceeds of industry? We in the C.C.F. say without question, the one who has the greater claim is the one who is doing the fundamental job of producing wealth. Yet we have not been able to sell that idea far enough, not only in this house but throughout Canada.
The situation in the future is going to be aggravated. It is going to become much more acute than it has been in the past, and for this reason. There is a new word being coined. It is coming into the English language, and it is called automation. I do not like these new words, but I do not know what other substitute there could be for this situation in which machines are displacing men. This is not new in industrial history. There has been progress because machines displaced men, although it should be noted that the progress was always at the expense of one group in the community, that group which could not protect itself.
Now, machines are displacing men at a rapidly accelerated rate. Automation is occurring far faster than was the case in the past. Let me give you one example, and there are many others which we could find if we were to look at industry. This is a situation which existed at the Chrysler plant in Detroit. There was an operation for the making of rocker arm supports, an operation

which included drilling, reaming and cutting. Five men were employed on two machines in this particular phase of the operation. These five men and two machines were able to produce 38 pieces an hour. Another machine has been brought in, so that one man and one machine can now manufacture 750 pieces an hour. In other words, a bank of the old machines could be rendered useless and 80 men could become unemployed because of this new piece of equipment and a social problem created.
Today we have to find the answer. The situation is more serious in the United States just now than it is here, but it is going to visit us in Canada. We cannot avoid it because there has to be progress. We may perhaps have to consider carefully how rapidly we progress, and in what way. If automation becomes more prevalent than it is today, the unions are going to find themselves in a position where seniority will count for nothing. The unions are going to find that job classification will go out the window because there will be no such thing in a mechanized society. Automation will certainly be here in our own lifetime. If this occurs the older worker, and by that I mean the man of 45 and over, is going to be unemployed. He is not going to be able to find work unless the fiscal policy of the government is such that, in some way or other, work is provided. There are, therefore, startling dangers ahead of us, and they are dangers because our political and economic thinking still lags lamentably behind the technology of the age. This thinking has to be brought up to date.
There may be an answer, perhaps, in the union request for a guaranteed annual wage. I certainly support the idea. I have heard it argued, on the other hand, that the guaranteed annual wage would be most unfair to management because management would be compelled to keep workers on their staff when no work was available. I should like to see management acting as bird dogs for a change. I am not altogether impressed with the quality or calibre of management in Canada. It is time they went out and did some rustling, not only to get orders but to make sure the men who are in the plants are being given employment.
Furthermore, a guaranteed annual wage may at last bring home to industry the responsibility it has to society. It is regarded as right, proper and prudent for industry to create a depreciation reserve for its fixed assets. Why is it not equally proper, prudent and wise to create a depreciation reserve for the human assets who are producing the wealth in the various plants throughout Canada? It is starting. We see signs of it here
The Address-Mr. A. Stewart and there, but not in adequate quantities. Industry has to take a greater social responsibility for the men whom it employs. If the government, through its injurious fiscal policies, creates unemployment the government representing society as a whole has to take responsibility for that.
There should be none of this nonsense of striking a man off unemployment benefits because he has been unemployed too long and there is still no work for him. I am not suggesting the guaranteed annual wage is the complete answer because I do not believe it is. I hope, however, the Department of Labour is considering this problem which is arising, and will meet with the unions and management in this country as soon as possible to try to devise some answer.
There is one other matter about which I want to speak, and one about which every member of the house feels quite as strongly as I. I am not quite certain yet about the members of the cabinet. I am thinking about the plight of the burnt-out veterans. I suppose other members had the same experience I had when I was home in that I was asked on a number of occasions to meet the Canadian Legion and say what I thought of the situation. I may as well say here what I thought. I thought the government's conduct was shoddy and shabby. I said it and I still believe it. I am prepared to withdraw those words when I see the new legislation introduced.
I think the conduct of the Canadian people, also, may have been shoddy and shabby when we consider their responsibility, because these were men who volunteered to fight to keep the skins of the Canadian people intact. We were in danger, so we would pay anything for our safety. Of course, once we became safe, we forgot about our moral obligation to those who had suffered for us. I hope the government is going to turn that moral obligation into hard dollars and cents when the new legislation comes down. All these people are asking for is justice; they are not asking for too much because I have said in the past, and I say again, the briefs of the Canadian Legion have been exemplary in the sense that they have asked for what was fair and nothing more.
Another thing: I hope this legislation will include some provision whereby the burnt-out pensioner is not, in effect, denied the old age pension when he achieves the age of 70. It can be said he is not denied the old age pension, he gets it. He has a right to it, certainly, but his pension is cut down by the amount he gets and his total income is not one iota greater afterwards than before. While technically he gets the old age pension, in

The Address-Mr. Garland effect he sees nothing of it. I hope the government will not be so miserable as to keep that regulation in force.
I should like to read a letter which I received. I have a great number of them, and I picked this one at random out of the file. It expresses very adequately what these old veterans feel. It is from 769 Atlantic avenue, Winnipeg, and reads:
The veterans are making a most justifiable appeal to the government of Canada, to seriously consider their appeal for an increase in their allowance and I am asking you being our member of parliament to give it your full support and consideration.
I most assuredly do.
The amount received is not sufficient for our expenses, having to meet the increased costs on all sides. Also hospitals and doctors if our wives are ill, more or less as the case may be, making a serious demand on the allowance. It is very reasonable that a married man receiving a veteran's allowance should be able to bring his income to $2,000 per year.
That is a most reasonable request. This next sentence is one which has a sting in it for all of us.
This is not too much to ask of a government who now pensions its M.P.'s at $3,000 per year.
The government of Canada recognizes that an income of $2,000 per year is too low for a married man to pay income tax.
I therefore feel that this figure is the lowest reasonable figure to ask as an income for the veteran who is no longer able to perform steady employment.
Your support in this matter is solicited with deep sincerity. Anything you can. do to bring the government recognition of its responsibility to the class of veterans affected will bring you the thanks and appreciation of ail veterans.
I would be very happy to see this appreciation transferred to the shoulders of the government; and it can be easily transferred by bringing in the sort of legislation which has been asked for by veterans and which has been asked for by members on all sides of the house. And if the government is prepared to do it, then I for one, and for a very brief time, am prepared to forgive the government for some of its obvious inadequacies.

Mr. Speaker, rising to participate in this debate, may I forgo the usual custom of long and flowery congratulations to the mover (Mr. Leduc) and the seconder (Mr. Carrick). May I say simply to them and to the other new members introduced on Friday last that it is gratifying to know that the membership of this House of Commons, with its unrivalled opportunity for service, continues to attract Canadians of ability and integrity.
Before dealing directly with the speech from the throne I would like to comment on one piece of government business at our last session. I refer to legislation that made


the lending facilities of our chartered banks available for home construction. I have always taken a keen interest in housing. Being a firm believer in the advantages of home ownership, I was naturally interested in this new legislation.
In our last session I was surprised and disappointed with the opposition in some quarters to this move. Some rather prominent members of the opposition expressed their doubts as to the advisability of having our banks participate in this field, and I seem to recall the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Hees) in particular advising the nation that Canada's banks would not be able to provide funds for home construction and at the same time perform their regular functions. How wrong he was!
An examination of the financial statements of Canada's banks, and recent figures from Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, reveal that the banks have made loans in this new field amounting to some $170 million. This is a remarkable performance when one remembers that the legislation was only in effect for a few months of the banks' fiscal year; and, what is more important, more housing units were completed in the year just ended than ever before in our history. Now Canadians will welcome the reference in the throne speech indicating the government's intention to bring into operation, at the beginning of February, those provisions of the National Housing Act in which loans may be made for home improvements. It is evident to most that this proposed legislation will substantially improve housing conditions in this country.
Mr. Speaker, there is another matter of national importance and of special interest to the people I represent and to northern Ontario generally, and that is the trans-Canada highway. A survey of the progress of this important project in northern Ontario is not impressive. I recognize the magnitude of this development and can understand the pressures and needs from the more densely populated areas of southern Ontario for a larger share of the highway dollar. I also recognize the difficulties the Ontario government has been having with their highways department, and I do hope that now, since the premier of our province has apparently found it necessary to intervene personally in this department, we can properly expect more emphasis on construction in northern Ontario. Our people expect and need this fine project completed as soon as possible. The continued development of northern Ontario is dependent on this road.
The further expansion of our tourist industry, the opening up of new areas giving

transportation facilities to new mining and lumbering developments both present and future, point up the need for the early completion of the trans-Canada highway through northern Ontario. May I remind the house that the agreements with the provinces were signed back in April, 1950, and are due to expire December 9, 1956. This leaves less than two years, and it is my sincere wish that every possible priority be given this important project by the government of Ontario and, indeed, all the provinces. After all, the federal treasury is paying 50 per cent of the costs, and the Canadian people expect action. If the necessary co-operation is not immediately forthcoming, I would suggest the federal government taking a firmer attitude with the provinces.
Another matter of concern is the early construction of a natural gas pipe line through northern Ontario. We are pleased to learn from the press recently that Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Limited now plan a more northern route to serve northern municipalities, with a spur line from North Bay to other important northern Ontario centres. Anything this house does to expedite this matter will be appreciated by northern Ontario.
There is another subject, Mr. Speaker, of direct concern to the people of Nipissing, that needs the attention of our Department of Public Works, and I take advantage of the opportunity afforded members in this debate to discuss local matters. I refer now to the docking facilities at North Bay and Sturgeon Falls. I am not going to remind this house that the district of Nipissing is truly a tourists' paradise-this is already well known. I need scarcely remind hon. members of the excellent facilities throughout our district. The Ontario Northland Boat Lines operate an excellent boat, the Chief Commando., daily during the navigation season, from the North Bay wharf. The rapid expansion of the tourist industry in Nipissing is causing an ever-increasing flow of traffic over the present facilities.
Important mining activities on the islands of lake Nipissing have further increased the flow of traffic. I have been successful in having repairs of a temporary nature done to both docks, and appreciate the co-operation received from the department. However, the time has come for extensive repairs to make sure that these important facilities are adequate for present-day traffic requirements.
It is not my intention to deal with many of the subjects contained in the speech from the throne. Most Canadians will approve the proposed amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act immediately to assist our citizens who, through no fault of their own, may 50433-11
The Address-Mr. Garland be unemployed this winter. And I am pleased this legislation is now under way. Canadians generally will approve the government's intention to amend the War Veterans Allowance Act, to raise the basic rates as well as the ceiling on permissible incomes of allowance recipients.
There will be general approval of the government's proposal to lower the age of eligibility and raise the income ceilings of Canada's blind citizens. Canadians will now have the right to expect humanitarian treatment for her disabled citizens. Too long, now, has this been a dark chapter in our program of social welfare.
Located as we are in Nipissing, so close to the gold mining country, and dependent on it for a substantial share of our economic wellbeing, we are anticipating continued support to that important industry through the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act. Further, I am sure all those interested in municipal affairs will await with keen interest the proposed amendments to the Municipal Grants Act.
I am not unmindful of Canada's activities and our responsibilities abroad in the fields of diplomacy, co-operative defence and assistance to underprivileged areas, plus a genuine desire and need further to promote freer world trade. Our government is keenly aware of these tremendously important problems and I can see no useful purpose in my discussing them at this time.
During the next several days we will undoubtedly hear much criticism of the speech from the throne, and that is as it should be in a democracy. Our socialist friends will argue that the benefits forecast in the speech are thoroughly inadequate. They will undoubtedly urge the launching of a huge program of public works, as though the benefits come automatically with the spending of public money. This seems to be the socialists' chief answer to current unemployment.
Our Progressive Conservative friends, on the other hand, will, as usual, talk about what it does not contain, and will no doubt take the position that spending of the kind recommended by the socialists will not correct the employment situation, and will only add to the already high prices of goods and services which the Progressive Conservatives claim is the real problem in the Canadian economy.
Sir, as a "middle of the roader", if such an expression is permissible, I suggest the answer, as is so often the case, lies somewhere between these two points of view. The spending of public money on well-planned and urgently needed public projects and services is necessary, and can make an important
162	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Garland contribution to our economy. But I suggest that this parliament approach our problems at this time calmly and confidently. Let us not be pushed into hastily conceived schemes. May I suggest that while this is not a time for complacency, neither is there any justification for gloom-peddling or any artificial pump-priming of our economy, or special preferred attention to a selected few.
In my opinion, our economy withstood the shocks of 1954 in surprisingly good fashion. The market for our staple wheat exports suffered a real slump. The United States experienced a sizeable recession that quite naturally took the edge off our prosperity here. There was a poor wheat crop in the west. These unfavourable circumstances were quite beyond the control of Canadians, yet we find new investment continuing at a high level. Our exports were reduced only by about the equivalent of the drop in wheat sales. Our other exports were just about maintained. In spite of the normal difficulties of Canadian exporters, a more favourable balance between exports and imports was achieved in 1954 than in 1953. This result, in my opinion, makes nonsense of all the clamour we hear that high Canadian costs are pricing us out of world markets.
Perhaps "makes nonsense" is rather strong language. Perhaps I should say that it punches plenty of holes in the sweeping charge that high Canadian costs are pricing us out of world markets. Let us remember that costs are only one factor that go into a sale. Let us remember that there are others. There is the question of availability. There is the question of quality and the question of aggressive sales approach. In the case of appliances and machinery there is the question of a good service organization behind an aggressive sales organization.
I am not suggesting that these factors do not exist, but one should not accept the general statement that high costs are our only problem in trade. Let us not forget that also in the late 1940's and the early 1950's we enjoyed markets that had never been traditionally ours, and it is only natural that since these countries have come back from the devastation of war they are going to be able to supply the products that they normally supplied. While we shall lose some markets, it is true, we are going to gain others and this is particularly true of our forest products in many countries of Europe. It is particularly true of base metals in many countries in Europe. I believe there are figures showing that the exports of these two commodities I have mentioned have increased in some months during the past year


to as high as 30 per cent or 35 per cent over the corresponding months of 1953.
Let us look for just a moment at the future. This Liberal government should seek to improve the already excellent relationship between business and government in Canada, and should continue to offer every possible incentive to new and existing business, as it is only through steady expansion of our free enterprise system that we can continue to improve the living standards of our people.
At the same time, we must recognize that at this halfway mark in the century we have reached the stage of development where those that have must share a part of their good fortune with those less fortunate, so that all of us may have more of the good things of life.
I suggest we have reached this stage in our international thinking as well as at home. Such a policy is reasonable and right, and is bound to find favour with free, fair-minded people everywhere. Such a policy I will continue to support in the firm belief that Canada can move forward to an even brighter future.
This policy of freedom for business, and social security for our people, has been inconsistent with Tory and socialist thinking alike, down through the years. To them, such a policy of co-existence could only be tolerated in cases of extreme emergency. To me, this combination of free enterprise and social welfare is the very cornerstone of the Liberal approach, and that is why the Liberal party continues to enjoy the confidence of fairminded Canadians everywhere.
At six o'clock the house took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The house resumed at eight o'clock.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in spite of all its carefully chosen words and limited demands, the speech from the throne could hardly be expected to suppress the fact that there is mounting unemployment at the present time in Canada. This is an ugly fact that stares us all in the face. It is a condition of our national economy that in my judgment will not be remedied by the building of ferries, the construction of an odd harbour, the removal of Ripple Rock, the building of historic sites and monuments and the like.
I think it is high time that we as members of parliament addressed ourselves seriously to the problems facing Canada with respect to production and trade. As that is going to be a most important subject during this particular session, I would like to go back and review a little bit of historical background relative to trade and tariffs.
The year 1914 closed an era. One world then died and another is still struggling to be born. That old world was dominated by one great country that had coal, limestone, ore and other basic resources close to the seaboard, and these provided the sound basis for an industrial economy which spread itself throughout the agricultural and raw material areas of the world.
The central fact about Britain's industrial economy was that she was first in the field and thus able to develop a tremendous lead over all possible rivals. In fact until the very latter part of the nineteenth century she had no industrial rivals at all. The British made money, therefore, by buying raw materials as cheaply as possible and selling against all comers in free markets, the countries to whom they were selling not having the facilities to manufacture industrial goods.
Today the industrial centres of production cannot be counted on the fingers of one hand. Two-thirds of the population of the world still remains peasant and poor, but in the other third industrial development in most cases has changed and is changing the social pattern of life, and has rescued and is rescuing nations from poverty in constantly widening areas.
50433-lli
have agricultural surpluses when so many are in need of food? The simple answer is that these countries in need of food have not yet been able to organize their resources and their political systems so as to be in a position to buy food. As you know, we do have the Colombo plan.
It is a truism that predominantly agricultural nations are poor. It is almost now a platitude to say that it is research and the industrial improvements that follow that transform our agriculture, our forest and mining industries into enterprises that provide more profitable occupations. Industrial development keeps our economies in a constant state of peaceful revolutionary change, and thereby provides better working conditions and better real incomes for all the individuals and families of our population.
Today we should have a searching look at our Canadian economy. That means we should glance backward and look forward. It is by looking at the wake of a ship that you can best discern the direction in which the ship is going. It is by taking a look at Canada back to the time of confederation that we are able to see the course on which our national economy was set some 85 years ago.
The first prime minister of Canada was Sir
John A. Macdonald. Following confederation there was a brief period of political consolidation, but in 1888 Sir John realized the lonely isolated economic position into which our economy was drifting. We had enjoyed very valuable preferences in agriculture and in shipping in the British market, to which our imber products at that time were making fotn*' contributions. But between 1846 and 1870 Britain had transformed herself into a free market economy and we were on the same basis in that market as all other countries of the world.
The United States had fought the Civil War and thereby swung the southern states into the industrial orbit of the north. Reciprocity which we had enjoyed with them, was abrogated. We were on our own. We had no real chance to develop native industries because of the much superior technological ability to produce possessed by other countries, especially the United States. Difficulties were on the horizon everywhere facing our producers of farm and other raw materials In these circumstances Sir John A. Macdonald moved his now famous resolution in the House of Commons on March 12, 1878, on going into committee of supply, and this I will read:
This house is of the opinion that the welfare of Canada requires the adoption of a national policy which, by a judicious readjustment of the tariff!
184	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. J. W. Murphy
will benefit and foster the agricultural, the mining, the manufacturing, and other interests of the dominion; that such a policy will retain in Canada thousands of our fellow countrymen who are now obliged to expatriate themselves in search of the employment denied them at home; will restore prosperity to our struggling industries, now so sadly depressed; will prevent Canada from being made a sacrifice market; will encourage and develop an active interprovincial trade; and moving (as it ought to do) in the direction of a reciprocity of tariffs with our neighbours, so far as the varied interests of Canada may demand, will greatly tend to procure for this country, eventually, a reciprocity of trade.
Note the last part of the resolution, which may appear today to have been brave words at the time. Sir John's resolution clearly implied we cannot have reciprocity with the United States until we set our own house in order; until we got into the habit of processing our own industrial and raw materials, and until in time we will be able to meet the United States on some reasonable ground of nearly equal competitive terms.
Thus we had, particularly in these two central provinces of Ontario and Quebec, the beginnings of what are now vast industries that can compete on nearly equal terms with any other country in the world. Most of our long-established industries can produce goods, pay salaries almost as high as anywhere else-I think as high as anywhere else with the possible exception of the United States-and put our goods on the world markets just as efficiently as other industrial countries.
The Conservatives were called upon to quit in 1896 and the Liberals, under the great Sir Wilfrid Laurier, took over until the year 1911. The Liberal party came into power on a trade platform which threatened to sweep away protection in Canada by promising to restore free trade on the model of industrial Britain. But when they came into power they became realists. It is true that they gave a voluntary preference to Britain, but Britain was not the great industrial threat to our native industry. It was the United States. At all events the national policy of Sir John A. Macdonald was so well safeguarded by the Liberals in power that the tariff structure which they left behind them in 1911 remained unchanged through the administrations of Borden and Meighen. There were some special war duties, but they were repealed as soon as the war ended.
If you compare the actual tariff exactions levied during the Laurier regime and the later regimes of Borden and Meighen, you will find that taken as percentage totals of all imports they vary by less than a fraction of one per cent, and generally speaking the same tariff which was accepted by the
IMr. Murphy (Lambton West).]

Laurier government in 1896, maintained by the Borden and Meighen governments from 1911 to 1922, was still good enough to survive the verbal onslaught of the Liberal leader who was prime minister of this country for over 20 years. So the Macdonald policy, in developing industry, became and remained the cornerstone of Canadian economic policy.
Up until the war of 1914 the development of industries and courageous immigration policies in our country and others maintained a healthy demand for primary products, and an especially wholesome demand for farm products. There were no difficulties in finding markets for farm products up until a year or two following world war I. But, of course, inevitably the war geared agricultural production to a point that could not be sustained in the face of the shrinking demand for agricultural products that followed the war.
The United States took swift action to protect its agricultural industry. In the early twenties we had the Fordney-McCumber tariff which disastrously cut the volume of our farm and fish exports. A post-war depression in those days seemed to be taken for granted, and in the middle twenties, after an industrial shakedown and temporary unemployment, Britain returned to the gold standard and the industrial process was again in healthy and rampant stride.
For reasons I do not wish to go into now at length this world economy which was promising so much, particularly to those optimists who were investing in the stock market-and weren't we all-collapsed in 1929. The United States congress again acted promptly. They enacted the Hawley-Smoot tariff which all but obliterated what remained of our farm export market. They followed this in 1932 with a special revenue act putting specific tariff duties against such metals as copper and such other primary products as lumber.
Mr. R. B. Bennett was then prime minister of Canada and, in different and even more difficult circumstances, he faced the same problem as Sir John A. Macdonald.
Canada was refused entry into the United States of her agricultural surpluses and her metals and lumber, and Britain, with the exception of some 100 special and not very high duties imposed during the war and postwar period, was operating on a free trade basis.
Mr. Bennett invited the nations of the commonwealth and empire to a conference in Ottawa. In the meantime Britain was forced off the gold standard and reverted to a substantial tariff structure ranging on industrial products from 10 to 33 and in some cases up to 50 per cent.

Most of the discussion about the empire agreements at that time centred on the secure and sheltered market we were guaranteed for portions of our agricultural products in Britain, but, as I see it now, the great gain that flowed from these agreements was the stimulus it gave to Canadian manufacturing industries.
As I pointed out, the British tariff on manufactured goods ranged from 10 to 33 and even up to 50 per cent, and as a result of the empire agreements our manufactured products were admitted into that country free.
What did this mean? It meant that United States industry selling to Britain would have to pay these rates I have just mentioned, whereas, if they moved their plants into Canada, or established branches in Canada, the products of these plants entered Britain mainly free of duty. You can go through Ontario or elsewhere in Canada today and you will see industry after industry which obtained a footing in this way and as a result of this development are now flourishing and supplying markets at home and abroad.
What we should all try to escape from is the state of academic anaemia in which our discussions on trade policy are conducted. In face of the record I have mentioned, what is the use of discussing free trade as a practical political proposition? All such discussion does not alter the fact that there is no genuine free trade party in Canada and there never was.
Since we have a tariff for protection, why not be fair and reasonable about its application? Why should industries which have entered Canada at the request of the government to supply vitally needed war materials, and which now employ many thousands of Canadian workers at the best prevailing rates of pay, be made the victims of hypocritical trade philosophy? That is the trouble about this double-talk regarding protection for industry.
The industries which can exert effective political pressure on the government are able to break through the sound barrier erected by the alleged free traders. Industries that are anxious to get on with their business and take fair and equitable treatment for granted are sacrificed on the altar set up by the academic free traders.
Because of our recent discoveries in natural resources, including gas and oil, we are in the process of developing a huge chemical empire in this country. This chemical industry has already been highly developed in the United States. Some products of these and other industries are admitted into Canada free from the United States, and similar
The Address-Mr. J. W. Murphy products going from Canada to the United States are subjected to substantial customs tariff rates.
When a given product is produced both in Canada and in the United States, and the government across the border levies customs duties and other imposts much in excess of ours, such a situation should become a matter for adjustment between the two countries. Canada's exports are fettered by foreign tariff regulations while, on the other hand, Canadian industry is exposed to damaging competition.
After the war we had visions of drawing all the nations of the world into various forms of collective action which were to be the sure road to a political world paradise. All nations banded together were to be as happy and peaceful as a basket of kittens. We now know that some of the kittens turned out to have long claws.
Let us not despair in the task of finding real avenues to a restored world order. But let us work with practical means towards practical ends. We are standing by the general agreement on tariffs and trade, while others are not. Our dairy products are subject to quota and our coarse grain products are either placed under quota or subjected to voluntary quota agreements. Devices are found within the terms of the agreements to protect domestic manufacturers. We take no advantage of such, while others do.
The ideological struggle between communism and democracy has led to the popular use of the expression "co-existence". In my opinion Canada should seek a revision of the Geneva trade agreement on the basis of Canadian industrial co-existence. By that I mean that out of an appreciation of a definite national purpose we should look to the recasting of our trade agreements to the degree that Canadian industry is allowed the right to live, even as our trading partners will seek the same right for their industries.
This, in essence, is what I mean by coexistence: the safeguarding and successful existence of Canadian industries which must, of necessity, compete with foreign industries which perhaps have advantages of labour, wage rates, and many other considerations.
We cannot pursue an inflexible policy which stifles industry and denies labour an opportunity of steady employment. Foreign exporters to Canada and Canadian industries cannot expect to sell much to unemployed Canadians.
Our domestic producers pay an excise tax of up to 15 per cent, and on top of that a further sales tax of 10 per cent. The Canadian manufacturer of automobiles pays excise and sales taxes totalling 25 per cent, against
166	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. J. W. Murphy the manufacturers across the line who pay an excise tax of 7 per cent. It is no wonder automobiles are cheaper in the United States.
We have an unemployment problem that will not be cured by public works or by subscribing to some bogus theory of free trade. It will be solved by giving good sound industrial enterprises a chance to compete on fair terms with industries abroad. In other words, an opportunity of co-existence.
A policy which levies excessive taxation on industry prices its products out of the market, adds new burdens to the cost of living, causes unemployment in Canada, and is obviously not good enough.
Japan and Germany are rising out of the ashes of defeat. Their standards of pay are not such as our workers will accept, and we do not want them to accept such standards. India looms across the horizon. What we need urgently now is a reappraisal of our national policy which has been accepted by all political faiths.
The general agreement on tariffs and trade is now up for revision. We are now in a position to make a reappraisal of its benefits and disadvantages to Canada.
Formerly we got on pretty well by making agreements with individual nations. In each case the effects of the agreements could be fairly forecast by the interested parties, by our trade experts, and by those who speak for the consumers at large.
Admittedly, GATT, which represents a general trade device that ties us all to a theory that does not always work out in practice, presents vastly new problems for our experts who advise the government in such matters.
Many members of the house were disturbed by the statement made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) after his return from Geneva. He seemed to think that the end of the world had come, in so far as international trade on a broad scale is concerned.
Let me say at once that we believe that the most earnest efforts should be made by this government to maintain the general structure of tariffs and trade agreements that were worked out in the first instance at Geneva, and which are now generally known as GATT. We, like most other signatories to this agreement, have two objects in mind. We want reasonably legitimate competitive safeguards for industries that are established in this country, and for industries, although now in their initial stages of development, that give real promise of becoming the means for profitable employment in this country. And we want markets for our surplus products.


The United States is now concerned about the problem of assuring itself of an adequate supply of key materials, especially minerals, and these at the lowest possible cost consistent with security factors.
Many of their needed products are produced in abundance in Canada. The United States more and more will become dependent on our imports of copper, lead, zinc, and iron ore. We, in the meantime, are dependent on them for coal and for citrus fruits. The coal problem is somewhat mitigated by the development of our oil and gas resources. We need their cotton. But in this day of substitution, we do not know how long that need, based on United States production, will last. One certain thing is that we were selling them large quantities of iron ore and we were buying from them large quantities of steel in the form of ingots and finished goods. They will continue to rely on us for supplies of nickel, asbestos and tin. Canada has the materials the United States needs. Canada has the basic materials, aluminum, iron ore, uranium, pulp, paper and lumber.
Our location gives us a major advantage in competing with the United States, and from a security point of view we are considered their best source of supply. We enjoy their confidence. Their investments in Canada have been richly rewarded over the years.
With the United States, and more particularly with our sister nations of the commonwealth, and in co-operation with the free nations of the world today, we must seek to re-establish orderly trade. Nationalism is still the most potent force in the world and what we must do is seek the great objectives of world security on the basis of enlightened self-interest. We shall not be true to the trust that is ours if we do not continue to process greater percentages of our base metals in Canada. We cannot be content to be hewers of wood and drawers of water. We can do as others do-and what is today the accepted basis of trade-namely, appraise our strength as a trader and obtain markets for these surpluses-especially in agricultural products-which we cannot use, and admit articles on a basis that does not destroy our standards of wage payments and our standard of living.
Finally, let me say this. We shall be false to our trust, and false to the best interests of Canada, if we continue to invite useful industries into Canada and then, for no good practical reason, have them slaughtered on the altar of an academic free trade policy.
If the dour predictions of the Minister of Trade and Commerce prove to be correct, we

will be on the verge of a jungle war in international trade, and the people of this country will expect the government to work out plans with the commonwealth, with the United States, and with as many of the free nations of the world as possible to regain our lost markets for our surplus products in this country.
