Mr. Speaker, there are a few comments that I should like to make at this time because I feel that this debate should play an extremely valuable role since it provides members on all sides of the house with an opportunity of turning the spotlight on what they consider to be the most important issues in their respective constituencies.
After having read carefully the speech from the throne, I fail to see where the government has given consideration to what I believe to be the most pressing problems facing the Canadian people at the present time. The government apparently has chosen to ignore the basic economic problems and is hoping that, by giving a few pieces of worthwhile legislation of a minor character-that is in terms of the whole economic picture- the people of the country will be satisfied. I suggest that in the government's approach to its legislative program this year they have given us no reason to believe that they are going to make any frontal attack on the most important problems which we face at the present time.
I feel a debate of this kind gives members an opportunity of expressing something of their basic philosophy and of their over-all approach to the problems of the government. One or two other members who have spoken in this debate have referred in a brief manner to this important aspect, namely the whole attitude of the government towards the legislation and its whole attitude towards the role of government in society.
There are in this country those who believe that the activities of the government should be restricted to an extremely narrow sphere. There are those who believe that the less the government has to do, in so far as the economy is concerned, the better off the Canadian people are. I find it difficult to understand why those who champion the cause of free enterprise deem it necessary to support such things as the anti-combines legislation and all sorts of government legislation which was placed on the statute books for the particular purpose of defending the people of Canada against the big business interests of this country. Indeed, if the champions of free enterprise were to follow their own belief to a logical conclusion, then I am sure that
The Address-Mr. Ellis the people of this country would find themselves in a much more serious position than that in which they find themselves today. Indeed in a democratic society the people have a right to look to the government not only for protection against economic interests over which they have little or no control, but also to give them some direction, some leadership, in the solution of economic problems. This concept of government is not new. Abraham Lincoln once described the government's role to be one of doing for the people what they were unable to do for themselves. As time goes on and our society becomes more complex, I believe the need for the continued attention of the government is selfevident. If you were to ask a man who is unemployed today, and who has done his level best to find employment, what he thinks of that concept of government, I am quite certain he would say, "I have done all I can for myself and must look to the government for some help to obtain employment". I think that is the logical and sensible way of viewing the activities of government today.
Now, we in this movement believe that in a democratic society the government which represents the people has a duty and responsibility to care for the interests of the people as a whole. The other day some hon. members referred to the credit union movement. I as a member of the co-operative movement, and as a member for some years of a credit union, wholeheartedly agree. There is a case where people, realizing that in our vicious economic system it is necessary to band together for mutual self-protection, are doing just that in a limited manner. What we in this movement argue is that the same principle applies to the economic machinery of this country as a whole. What we want in democratic society is a greater measure of democratic control of the economy.
There is planning in this country. Hon. members talk about the dangers of planning. It would be impossible to carry on a modern government without a great degree of planning. Our whole economic machinery in this country is planning. The big question is not whether or not we are going to have planning; the question is who is going to do the planning and on whose behalf. We argue that whatever planning is done should be done in the interests of the people of this country, not planning by corporations designed to enhance the fortunes of this or that particular group of companies. We know that in this complex society in which we live there has to be planning. We in this movement insist it should be democratic planning by a democratic government in the interests of all the people of the country.
168	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Ellis
Earlier 1 mentioned that in my opinion the government has completely ignored the basic economic difficulties facing the people of this country. I want to refer to just two or three signs of that unwillingness to face up to reality. Coming as I do from a constituency which depends entirely on the prosperity of the surrounding agricultural area, I am very much alarmed by the falling off of our external trade and the serious decline in net farm income. I cannot view with anything but seriousness the fact that in the past year our exports of Canadian wheat and other coarse grains has declined by some 40 per cent. When you translate that fact into its broader implications throughout Canada it is easy to understand why there have been widespread lay-offs in the farm machinery industry, why industrial activity is down, and why we find many industrial workers unemployed.
In addition to the falling off of agricultural exports we know that for the first ten months of last year there was a decline in the value of merchandise exports by approximately 8 per cent. These are signs which the government ought to take into consideration. The government should realize they are danger signs which must be faced if we are to avert an even more serious economic condition in this country. I can recall attending political meetings in my own province where the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) and Liberal spokesmen have answered the question of the lost British markets by saying, "Look at our trade position; we are doing wonderfully well." They completely ignored the fact that our trade position was based on the fact we were exporting agricultural commodities to the United States.
Anyone who wanted to view the situation objectively would know that the United States has never been, and will never be, a dependable market for farm products. I believe it was the editor of the Montreal Star who last week, speaking over the air, described the United States market as something like a water tap. If the United States producers were not able to meet the requirements of the domestic market and export trade, the government would turn on the tap and allow our Canadian products to enter the United States. But just as soon as the United States production was sufficient to meet the domestic requirements of that country and to take care of their export requirements, then of course the government would turn off the tap. Anyone who wanted to use a little bit of foresight and plain common sense could have seen that development coming.
Apparently this government, when it lost the British market, said, "Look, we have 

given you markets in the United States." They must have known we could not hope to keep those markets indefinitely. This is not without its serious effects on the economy of this country.
With respect to the falling net farm income we find that 1954 was the third successive year in which there has been a substantial drop in net farm income. During that period net farm income dropped from $2,115 million to $1,200 million, a drop of some 44 per cent. One cannot stress too strongly the seriousness of this disastrous drop in income, because the farmer plays a unique role in our economy. The farmer is not merely a producer of consumer goods, he is also the owner and operator of a relatively highly capitalized small business. In that dual role he is purchasing farm machinery and other capital goods. No survey has been made in this country to reveal the extent to which that is carried on, but research surveys have been made in the United States which indicate that the average farmer will purchase 2-4 times as much per capita as the consumer in the city.
Thus we find this disastrous drop in net farm income has a very serious effect on employment in the industrial areas of Canada. One cannot stress too strongly the interdependence of those who work the soil and those who work in our factories, offices and other places of employment.
This brings me to the third aspect, and one with which I should like to deal in a little more detail, the question of unemployment in Canada. One of the most discouraging features of the speech from the throne is the refusal to face up to the unemployment problem as it exists. The government tries to create the impression that unemployment does not exist in Canada. When they are placed in the position of having to defend themselves they say there is a little unemployment but it is only seasonal or only regional. They will try to pass it off as being of little consequence. Perhaps as supporters of the free enterprise system they believe a little unemployment is inevitable. Perhaps they take the attitude of some businessmen that not only is a certain percentage of unemployment inevitable under our system but that it is desirable. I do not know whether that is the thinking of the members of the government, but at any rate they do not seem to pay very much attention to the fact that some 500,000 or more-this year likely closer to 600,000-Canadians will be out of work.
The government does not consider that serious enough. Just how serious does the unemployment situation have to become

before the government recognizes it exists? Are they going to wait until there are
800.000	unemployed, one million unemployed or 1-5 million? Just where are they going to draw the line between concern and lack of concern? They have argued that unemployment is regional, that it is seasonal. We know that according to the national employment service last winter there were some
569.000	Canadians out of work. Last fall the Canadian Congress of Labour estimated that this winter there would be in excess of
600.000	persons in Canada out of employment. Yet the government feels that this is not serious enough to give closer attention to in its legislative program this year. We know that this unemployment is not concentrated in any one particular area, because we find unemployment in all parts of Canada. I have talked to members of the House of Commons from all parts of the country and I have heard the same story- "Unemployment is bad in my city"; "Unemployment is bad in our part of the country."
I say that some of the members on the government side of the house who get up and pat the government on the back ought to ask themselves the question as to how serious unemployment is in their own community. I would like to know how many government supporters are prepared to get up and say that there is no unemployment in their constituencies. I doubt if one of them can get up in this House of Commons and say that the unemployment situation is not serious in his area.
I would welcome the assurance to the house by the government supporters on this unemployment question, but we do know this, that we have the facts regarding unemployment. We know that unemployment has increased in the following industries: non-ferrous metal products, mining, shipbuilding, machinery, aircraft and parts, sawmills, construction, logging, clothing, railroad equipment, automobiles and parts, iron and steel, textiles and farm machinery. These are the basic industries of this country-particularly the steel industry.
As I say, these are the basic industries of Canada. There is mounting unemployment in these industries; yet the government feels that it is not important enough to make a frontal attack on the problem. With respect to the farm machinery industry, which is a striking example, there has been such a fall in net farm income that the farmers cannot buy new machinery. The result is that we find widespread unemployment in the farm machinery industry. We know that since 50433-12
The Address-Mr. Ellis 1952 there has been a reduction in farm machinery production to the extent of some 34 per cent.
Once again, the attitude of the government seems difficult to understand-this willingness on their part to ignore the seriousness of unemployment in this country. And with respect to the argument that unemployment is regional, as I have already pointed out, if anyone will make a survey of the country he will find unemployment right across Canada.
Just look at the records of the employment offices and they will indicate that unemployment is widespread from one part of Canada to the other.
And then, in connection with seasonal employment: of course we have always had seasonal employment in this country. And yet it is only in the last couple of years that we have had such great numbers of unemployed as we now have in the winter months.
Then, of course, just because a man gets a few months' work in the summer months is not an answer to the employment problem. I am sure that those men who are looking for employment want year-round employment. They want some measure of job security with decent working conditions and good wages. The government cannot take satisfaction from the fact that the unemployment figures might be a little higher in the winter than they are in the summer. What we want is employment all the year round; and in those areas where such employment is not available there should be other employment made available so that those who are doing seasonal work can take on other work in the off-season.
These are questions to which the government must give serious consideration. Then, with regard to the government's attitude concerning unemployment, I wonder why they refuse to admit the seriousness of the problem. I suggest the reason the government is not willing to face up to the unemployment problem is the simple fact that they have no plan or no solution for the problem; and they hope that by ignoring it they can muddle through, and that something will come along to pull them out of the economic swamp in which they find themselves at the present time.
Now, with respect to the official opposition, it was quite interesting last Monday to hear the speech of the Acting Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Rowe) and to remember that he alone, among the present members of his party in the House of Commons, was a cabinet minister in the government of the late R. B. Bennett. I do not think our memories are so short that we cannot cast
170	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Ellis our minds back over that period, during which time we had a Conservative government in this country. I believe the late Mr. Bennett went out to seek election and in a public meeting in Regina promised to end unemployment in 60 days, I believe it was, or 90 days-some such time, anyway.

Someone in the official opposition says that Mr. Bennett did end unemployment in 90 days. Well, I do not know whether he thinks that the relief camps were a solution to the unemployment problem of that time. But we do know that apparently that was the Conservative party's answer to unemployment: "Let us herd all the single unemployed into relief camps and get them out of the way, into the bush country. Let us remove them from their homes and put them in relief camps, in enforced idleness."
That was regimentation, if there ever was regimentation in this country. Hon. members who talk about regimentation in society must know that we had -the greatest regimentation during the time of the relief camps under the government of the late R. B. Bennett.
Then we had a change of government in 1935 when the Liberals took office. Well, they muddled along in 1936, 1937 and 1938, and nothing was done about the unemployment problem. It is true that they did away with the relief camps, but in place of those relief camps the young men were hounded about the country, driven from one city to another, kept one jump ahead of the vagrancy laws. Those who were fortunate enough to get direct relief got 50 cents a day, out of which they were supposed to house, feed and clothe themselves-all on 50 cents a day relief. And that was the Liberal party's answer to unemployment at that time.
Then the war came along, and apparently -that granted a reprieve. The great development in the industrial machinery of this country in connection with the prosecution of the war brought about a period for which they now take credit, and describe as a great period of prosperity. And then after the war, when the leading economists, when the spokesmen for the chambers of commerce and the various banks, along with members of the C.C.F., predicted that when the war ended and a transformation from a wartime to a peacetime economy had taken place we would be faced with a recession, and an


inevitable depression, the evil hour was put off. This was done first of all by the repairing of the ravages of war, indirectly by exports in connection with the Marshall plan, and so on, and then later through the development of the cold war followed by the great rearmament program and then Korea. All of these were artificial stimulants to the economy which managed to maintain a relatively high level of employment in this country.
But now, in spite of all that, in spite of the tremendous defence program, we are now faced with the fact that we have over half a million unemployed in Canada. And the government chooses to do nothing about it.
Now, with respect to the government's attitude toward the unemployed-

Someone says to take care of the Socreds. I have not mentioned them because, by their own choice, they have aligned themselves with our friends across the chamber, and with our Progressive Conservative friends to the right. They are the most vociferous element of free enterprise, and consequently have completely removed any possibility of attaining anything so far as reform is concerned.
I believe during the time that the late Mr. Bennett and the late Mr. Mackenzie King were wrestling with the unemployment problem in the thirties, in their own hearts they desired to see the end of unemployment. But they failed because their parties were committed to maintain the free enterprise system. And because they were tied to that system they found themselves powerless to grapple with the forces produced by it.
I hear some interruptions to my right, Mr. Speaker, but I have not been able to hear them clearly. I wish I could, and I would answer.
I suggest the reason the government has not been able to grapple with the problem today is that they are committed to the defence of the free enterprise system. We know that the Prime Minister quite rightly reminded the Acting Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Rowe) that they too were committed to a defence of the free enterprise system; and therefore offered no alternative. Concerning the economic problems faced by the people of this country, the failure of the government to deal with them would be matched by the failure of the official opposition to deal with them and the failure of the Socreds to deal with them, because any party which commits itself to a defence of free enterprise finds itself unable to deal with the problems facing the country at the present time.

Sir William Beveridge, in a study of the post-war situation in Great Britain, came to roughly the same conclusion, that within the narrow framework of free enterprise no solution was possible to our major economic difficulties. We in our group believe the health and the prosperity of the people of Canada to be more important than a slavish adherence to an outworn economic system. Because we believe that, we are in a position to offer policies that.will tackle and overcome the problems facing' Canada at the present time.
I realize it would be too much to expect the government to adopt our policies. That is too much to expect. I realize that after we have championed a cause for some considerable length of time and it grows in popularity with the Canadian people, when it reaches a certain stage then they are quite apt to reach out and embrace our program and our policies. We have even gone one step further. We have got to the stage where even the Conservatives are willing to reach out and embrace our policies. I believe the most interesting feature of the amendment offered by the Acting Leader of the Opposition was the fact that they now appear to be in favour of health insurance.

The Address-Mr. Ellis
One of my colleagues mentioned also the South Saskatchewan dam. I can think of no better example of a type of project that should be commenced at the present time than the South Saskatchewan river dam. I mentioned a moment ago that in a public works project only a small percentage in some instances of the actual money involved goes into the area in which the construction project is taking place. In any great construction project there is a great leakage; that is, in the purchase of machinery, the capital goods that are required to carry out the project. A great deal of the money spent on that project will be spent in buying machinery, in buying supplies in all parts of Canada.
With respect to the South Saskatchewan river dam, there are those who feel that the benefits of that would accrue only to the people of Saskatchewan. Such an idea of course completely flouts economic facts. In order to build that dam it will be necessary to purchase a great deal of heavy machinery. Where would that machinery come from? It will come from the industrial areas of Ontario and Quebec. Certainly that is going to be of great assistance to the industrial workers in those parts of the country. There are going to be all sorts of raw materials that will come from various parts of the country. Admittedly some of these raw materials will be purchased in the United States and perhaps in other countries, but the bulk of these purchases will be made in Canada, and the amount of money spent on that dam will be spread throughout the country to the benefit of the entire dominion, not of one particular area of the country.
Apart from the South Saskatchewan dam, there are many other projects that could be carried on at the present time. Someone in the official opposition said something about highways. I think we realize that in the United States all the main highways have been built by the federal government. Today we in Canada have a situation where highways are of national importance, and yet the contribution the federal government has seen fit to make to the construction of highways is its share of the trans-Canada highway, which is very inadequate. What the federal government should do is to undertake to be responsible for building the main highways across Canada, the main international and interprovincial highways in this country, thus relieving the provinces of great financial burdens in building and maintaining highways, particularly in those parts of Canada that are sparsely settled.
Then of course there is the question of railway level crossings. That is a matter

that should certainly receive the attention of the government. I know in my own city there is quite a number of extremely dangerous railway crossings and particularly along the main line of the railroad where there are double tracks.
These are some of the things which the government could be doing, but apparently they are prepared to sit back and do nothing and allow the situation to become progressively worse. My suggestion is that it is easier to deal with a problem now than a year hence or two years hence. What is needed now is a little bit of constructive planning, a little foresight which the government up to the present time has not shown. There are many others that could be suggested. Surely the government is in a position to know what the needs are in regard to public works projects across the country.
They could for example provide employment for a great many by the production of low rental housing units in various parts of Canada where the housing situation is most serious. There are many other worthwhile projects which could be undertaken by the government at this time if they were prepared to admit the seriousness of the unemployment problem. If they are not prepared to admit the problem exists, then it means that we in the opposition have to keep insisting that the government realizes the extent and the seriousness of the problem.
My closing suggestion to the government is once again that they offer some hope and assurance to the people of Canada that they are prepared to face up to the economic problems confronting the country at this time through a system of forward pricing, by some effort to provide parity prices for our farm commodities and by seeking through the means of public works projects to alleviate the immediate problem of unemployment where it exists in Canada.
The main thing is to agree now to assume responsibility for the employable unemployed in this country. No one province in this country is in a position to effectively tackle the problem on its own. Unemployment is a national problem. Indeed, one might argue that it is an international problem. Certainly it can be argued that it is an international problem in countries whose economies are as closely related as are those of the United States and Canada.
It is a national problem which must be met at the national level. I hope the government will not resort to its time-honoured strategy of passing the buck to the provinces and saying, "We will get together with the provinces and talk it over." They have talked

The Address-Mr. Shaw
it over for a couple of years and in the meantime a great many Canadians are in want, without employment and unable to maintain a decent standard of living.
Once again I suggest that the federal government must take upon its own shoulders responsibility for the condition in which we find ourselves today. Before the last election they were running around the country saying, "You have never had it so good. What a beneficent government we have down at Ottawa." You have never had it so good. Try telling one of the 600,000 unemployed that he has never had it so good. Try telling the farmers of this country who have been losing their markets that they have never had it so good. I am sure you will come in for a very rude awakening if you do.
In closing, I simply want to impress upon the government the necessity for immediate attention to these most serious problems. The people of Canada will await with a great deal of anticipation the activities of the government in this respect.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, frankly I was intrigued although amazed at certain statements made by the hon. member for Regina City (Mr. Ellis) during his address. He told us, by inference at least, that Abraham Lincoln was a socialist. It is rather surprising and amazing that it takes but one short speech to completely alter the facts of history.
I listened with a great deal of amusement while he was damning the Liberals and Conservatives and assuring the house and the country that they offered no hope and in the same breath asserting that they had stolen practically all that was good in the C.C.F. program. We are personally convinced that by virtue of that theft, if for no other reason, they offer little hope.
The speech of the hon. member reminded me of one that was delivered yesterday by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Regier), who took us into New Brunswick, then into Quebec and then back to British Columbia. Then in his spare time he commented on other things. I was reminded while listening to the hon. member's speech, and wanting to believe some of it, of last July when I was in Vancouver sitting in my car with the radio on. I had noted there was to be a program "Town Meeting in Canada" on the air, the subject to be discussed being co-existence, which of course embraced the general theme of whether it is possible for us to live in peace in the same world with the communists. During that program I heard the hon. member say that one of the Social Credit leaders in Ottawa had stated, I assume
in this house, that he wanted war. Remembering that, I could not take him seriously yesterday, nor could I believe very much of what he said.
I hope in my approach to current issues at this time I may be realistic, objective and fair. At least that is my desire. An examination of the speech from the throne does indicate certain bright spots. There is no question about that, and I would be the first to admit it. Reference was made to the Disabled Persons Act having been proclaimed to go into effect on January 1 of this year. We welcomed that act last spring and were glad to see it proclaimed. We are pleased to note that all the provinces of Canada have agreed to enter into agreements with the federal government.
However, I am extremely disappointed in one respect. I have been compelled to conclude that when the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) made so certain last spring that he would give only the minimum of information to the house, there was a reason for it. We questioned him -I did myself-with respect to the regulations which might be passed. Once again, I did not secure very much information. I find now that the regulations are so narrow and restrictive in character that were the government in my own province to drop its own act and operate only under the joint act 50 per cent of the people now receiving disability pensions in Alberta would be dropped completely from the rolls. That indicates how much more restrictive this new act is than the one which we have had in operation in Alberta for more than a year and a half. I regret that very much, because I had personal reasons to believe that in some respects our own provincial act was too restrictive in character.
The speech from the throne referred also to something with which we have dealt already, namely, certain amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act. I am not going to talk about them, since we have already expressed our views.
One thing that does concern us is that the government has taken the position that unemployment is only seasonal and regional in character. Is it the intention of the government to broaden its public works program only in those areas where the condition is known to be extremely serious? I trust that that will not be their approach to this problem.
For years we have pressed, as have the Legion, for amendments to the War Veterans Allowance Act. We are pleased to note that this act is to be amended, that the rates are to be increased, and that the amount of
174	HOUSE OF COMMONS
The Address-Mr. Shaw
permissive income will also be increased. However, I think I should serve notice now that it is going to be extremely difficult for us to be satisfied with anything less than the recommendations submitted by the Canadian Legion, because there is every reason to believe that their recommendations are realistic and are designed to meet current conditions.
We are also interested in noting that there are to be amendments to the Blind Persons Act. We understand the object of the amendments will be to lower the age of eligibility and raise the allowable income ceiling. We are in favour of this contemplated action, though I would not suggest at the moment that we are going to commit ourselves with respect to all the aspects of the amendments which the government may at a later date bring down. However, we approve of them in general.
We note that a joint committee is to be set up for the purpose of studying the Municipal Grants Act. Personally I am quite dissatisfied with the act as it now stands. Altogether too many deserving communities have been left out in the cold, and we trust that the committee may see fit to recommend a broadening of the base of this act so that it may go far beyond its present scope. In fact, I think good arguments could be advanced in support of the contention that it should cut completely across the board and cover all federal government installations within municipalities. I might well be asked whether I believe in the same thing from a provincial point of view; personally I do.
Those are not all the bright spots in the speech from the throne, but they are the only ones to which I will refer for the moment. Yesterday the hon. member for Westmorland (Mr. Murphy) made a plea for an extension of loans under the Canadian Farm Loan Act. He asked for a broadening of the regulations so that the act might apply within the province of New Brunswick. I have had some experience with the application of that act throughout Canada generally, and I believe there are certain very serious weaknesses. One is that the government, or the board charged with the operation of the act, in making its assessment of a farmer's land and chattels, seems to work on the theory that some time hence there is going to be a serious depression and that values will therefore be at a low level. Therefore, in assessing a farmer's property today for the purpose of determining whether they should authorize a loan they apply this fantastically low level of values. I am not blaming the persons who administer the act, because they are governed by the terms of the act itself and

its resulting regulations. But I have looked over certain applications and I am utterly amazed to see the low values being placed on land and chattels, the result being that hundreds if not thousands of Canadians are prevented from securing assistance under this act.
In fact, I have been compelled to come to the conclusion that the act was not designed to assist people who really require help, because in most of the cases I have examined I have come to the conclusion that those who should qualify could have got along very nicely without any assistance whatsoever. I mention that only in passing because, while I do not know anything about the New Brunswick situation, and I am not referring to that situation in particular, the hon. member's reference to this matter brought my own experiences to mind. 1 might add that the limited number of loans that have been made, and the small amount which has been made available through various loans, would indicate that there seems to be something seriously wrong with the operations of the act.
I wish to come back now to the question of unemployment. In the speech from the throne the government contended that it is seasonal and regional. As far as I am concerned I believe that that is the master understatement of the year. There is a certain amount of seasonal unemployment, it is true, and there is a certain amount of regional unemployment. There is some which one might designate as transitional unemployment, but there are strong indications that over and above this we are faced with a situation where altogether too many Canadians are unemployed and many of them see no hope in the foreseeable future.
The government has stated that there are approximately 300,000 registered unemployed in this country. But it has been pointed out more than once in this house that there are also probably an equal number who, for some reason or other, have never registered at all, and reliable statistics seem to bear that out. There are indications at the present time, and I shall elaborate upon this in a moment, that certain of our important industries have either collapsed or are in the process of so doing. I believe the coal mining industry is a pertinent example, and I will also refer to that later on.
In this regard I would refer to the very noticeable, marked decline in net farm income. I think it was my leader, the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low), who referred to this as the price cost squeeze. He was referring on the one hand to higher operation costs, and lower returns on the

other. This has caused a very uneasy feeling among the farmers of western Canada, and I am sure among farmers in other provinces as well. We also have a feeling of uneasiness resulting from the continuation of the unreasonably heavy burden of taxation which is certainly aggravating the situation.
The people of my constituency read with a good deal of interest the reported remarks of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) with respect to this matter. I cannot quote his words exactly but he did indicate that he was experiencing some concern on this matter, especially with that aspect of it dealing with sales and excise taxes.
In my part of western Canada we faced a rather difficult period last year, and as far as agriculture is concerned it was possibly a bit more difficult than is normally the case. These difficulties, in major parts, resulted from matters over which we have no control. For example, we had extremely wet weather, unusually heavy hail, and frost which struck the crops down prior to harvesting. But even worse, the frost came before the crops had ripened. Fortunately, while the picture looked extremely bleak around early October, the weather later changed and we were able to acquire the feed which is such an extremely important commodity in our mixed farming areas. The losses which have resulted have once again brought our farmers into direct conflict, if I may use the word in that sense, with our Prairie Farm Assistance Act.
A year or two ago I took a full 40 minutes to point out what I considered to be the existing weaknesses in the Prairie Farm Assistance Act, particularly as it applies to the non-drought areas of western Canada. That act is just not realistic in any sense at all. It fails utterly to do the job which I think it should be designed to do in that area. As I said before, I cannot think of one single, solitary thing that has caused more bitter comment with respect to this government than has that same Prairie Farm Assistance Act. Before many more months go by I hope that the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) may see fit to refer this act to the committee on agriculture with one important idea in mind, namely that of making it apply with some sense and reason to non-drought areas. I know that act must be a headache to all the men who try to administer it. I offer no criticism whatsoever of those men. I know many of them. They are trying desperately to do a good job, but they are trying desperately to do the impossible; and how frustrating that attempt must become. I say again to the Minister of Agriculture: For goodness' sake refer that act to the committee on agriculture and try to straighten out certain of those things.
The Address-Mr. Shaw
Speaking of unemployment and speaking of the collapse of industry, I am compelled to make reference to one rather tragic happening in my own constituency. Located about 120 miles west of Red Deer is a town called Nordegg; and located at Nordegg are the great Brazeau collieries, one of the most modern mines in western Canada. Following a disastrous fire about five years ago the above-ground installations were completely modernized and one of the finest briquetting plants was installed. It cannot be said by anyone that the mine has not operated efficiently either as a consequence of poor management or as a consequence of failure to modernize. It is modern and it has been managed well. In that community have lived more than 1,000 people. The coal produced in that area was a weather-resistant coal used for domestic heating, railway fuel and steam-raising in general. I do not know whether or not I have already mentioned this fact, but the capital value of the installation there is about $1,500,000.
This mine supplied fuel for the Canadian National Railways. Later it was reduced merely to providing station coal. In April of 1954, 200 men were laid off. Newspaper reports indicate that next Sunday the mine will close down, with another 150 miners becoming unemployed. As I say, you cannot blame the operators. Over the past year production there has been declining by
20,000	tons per month. Whether or not the mine will be opened again will naturally depend upon a number of things. With those miners laid off at Nordegg and with the closing of that mine, it looks as though a ghost town is going to develop. It is true that there is a certain amount of logging and lumbering in that area but it is not an industry of sufficient size to maintain that town. Not only is it a tragedy from the standpoint of miners and their dependents but personally I think it is a tragedy from the standpoint of the national welfare and safety. Within the last four years about 2,000 miners have lost their jobs out there as a consequence of mines closing.
Mr. Speaker, I approach this subject not with the idea of criticizing anybody but with the idea of trying to point out the necessity of speeding up our efforts to keep this industry alive. We know what have been the causes for the deterioration in that industry in Canada. There has been the loss of markets because of competitive fuels. There has been the replacement of railway locomotives by diesel units and conversion of coal-burning locomotives to oil burners. We know that oil and gas progressively have eliminated coal from our local and our industrial markets.
176	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Shaw We also know that excessive transportation costs have made almost impossible the capture and the retention of eastern Canadian markets for Alberta coal. We know also that the heavy importation of United States coal into central Canada has had a disastrous effect. More United States coal is imported into central and eastern Canada than is produced in western Canada. Production in 1953 alone in our Canadian coal industry was 1| million tons less than it was during the previous year, and recent statistics indicate further substantial decreases. If we are satisfied to let our coal industry fall into decay, all well and good; we are doing the right thing. But if we as Canadians believe that the future may demand an adequate coal supply-and certainly that is what I believe-we should keep our miners where they can continue in the only work which they are used to. If it is our desire to do that, then certainly we cannot allow that industry to fall apart.
We know that we have the dominion coal board. We know of the objectives which they set up in 1947; and those were good objectives. They were going to maintain an adequate supply of coal for all of our national requirements. Of course, it may be said that we have sufficient for our national requirements. They were going to support a sound and healthy coal-producing industry in Canada. Of course we have not just accomplished that objective. One of their purposes was the development of a steady and adequate market for the output of Canadian mines. We have not been able to do that. There was to be provision for fair wages and reasonably full employment for Canadian miners. Of course when we have had 2,000 of them become permanently unemployed out there, I believe, as far as miners are concerned, within the last four years, certainly we have not been able to maintain reasonably full employment. Then of course the board had as another objective, I believe, the extension of our markets for Canadian coal with the resultant saving of foreign exchange. Of course, instead of our finding extended markets for our western Canadian coal, we are losing markets. I am not blaming the dominion coal board at all. I am just trying to point out for our own benefit that while in 1947 we had five good objectives, with the exception of one we have just missed our mark completely. Personally I feel that the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys (Mr. Prudham) is concerned about this matter. He is an Albertan. This matter falls within his department. I know that his department, in co-operation with the Alberta government, has been doing certain things. The federal government has its subvention program. The


Alberta government, for example, has its fund for the rehabilitation of these men, among other things. We understand that the two are co-operating from a scientific point of view in an effort to find new uses, and consequently new markets, for this product. I have read the minister's statement, and I read all the debate which took place last June. I know from the statement of the minister that he feels, so he has said, that with a population of approximately 22 million at some future date, this country is going to need every source of fuel-I believe he said even firewood.
Anyone who understands the coal mining industry must realize that you cannot close these mines for long periods of time without serious deterioration, and in some cases they may become completely valueless and useless. If these experienced miners are to be removed and re-established in other lines of activity, it is highly possible that they will never go back to mining. Certainly, there is not very much chance of their sons ever taking up mining. Therefore, if what the minister states is true, that some time hence we will undoubtedly require all this fuel, it is going to be a very bleak picture if our mines cannot be put into operation because of deterioration and if we have to start to train miners, which is a long and hard process.
Now, when the gold mining industry in Canada showed some signs of deterioration and when the members from those areas spoke of the ghost towns that would develop, there was no hesitation on the part of this parliament in granting subsidies of $80 million, I believe. The united mine workers out there I believe asked the federal government to consider this question. They asked also that the federal government consider the question of restricting coal imports from the United States. I understand from a press report that a commission is presumably studying these two aspects of the problem.
I should like to know what developments have taken place up to date. Are there likely to be subsidies? Is the government likely to restrict the importation of coal from the United States? I understand also that a conference was held here last fall. I believe the miners themselves were represented, the operators were represented, the provincial government and the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys. I understand this whole matter was gone into rather thoroughly, and I should like to know what has resulted from that conference. I should like to know what has been done as a consequence of that conference. Let me repeat, Mr. Speaker, that I am not trying to place the blame. I know

the provincial government has a responsibility in this field. I know that the federal government has a responsibility in this field. I am not trying to place the responsibility. I am trying to emphasize the urgency of preserving this industry and of preserving the way of life of so many of these miners and their dependents. As I say, they have been added to this unemployment roll.
We have had some question raised as to whose responsibility the employable unemployed are. If someone were to ask me whose responsibility the employable unemployed are, I would give my answer. I would not find it difficult to agree with the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Philpott) who, in one of his columns which appeared in the Red Deer Advocate of December 1, 1954, had this to say:
It seems to me that there is one point on which nobody in Canada should quibble. The federal government is primarily responsible for full employment or non-full employment.
It is the federal authority, and only the federal authority, which has the necessary control over exports and imports, as well as over interprovincial trade. It is the federal authority alone which has the necessary power over taxes, money and credit.
Then he goes on:
Nobody in any political party has challenged the above principle for at least 20 or 25 years past.
Then he adds this:
It is a disgrace in this day and age that any decent citizen of Canada should be forced to choose between a soup kitchen and starvation.
Vancouver and other great cities of Canada have every right to demand that the federal government should stand behind them when it is necessary to give financial assistance to unemployed not eligible for unemployment insurance.
Now, I hope that the hon. member for Vancouver South will be able to sell this to all of his colleagues on the other side of the house. I find no cause to disagree with him, although I would probably be a bit more realistic and say I do believe the provinces and municipalities bear some responsibility too. We should not be so concerned about trying to pin down responsibility as we should be about getting all to assume full responsibility and to bring a solution to a problem that is certainly most serious.
Now, Mr. Speaker, as one who is firmly convinced that all speeches should be cut to about 30 minutes, possibly I should set a fairly reasonable example.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the beginning of each term, I usually speak thus to the students of Laval
The Address-Mr. Masse University: Whilst you are duty-bound by the university to attend my lectures, it is my duty to teach to the best of my ability, to be of service to you and the community at large.
Today, I find myself in the same position as far as my electors are concerned, because they have entrusted me with the task of making their feelings of loyalty known to the government of Canada. It is also my duty to bring their requests, their aspirations and their wishes to the attention of the government.
I must also congratulate the mover (Mr. Leduc) and the seconder (Mr. Carrick) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne, because they have been a credit to the electoral districts they represent and I am happy to offer them my sincere congratulations. They have faithfully served their respective constituencies.
Mr. Speaker, in the exercise of my profession, I have made it a point to examine loyally and dispassionately all situations and resolved never to form an opinion before giving the matter full consideration. I have been well served by this practice in the exercise of my profession, and I am happy to say that I have endeavoured to follow the same tactics in the discharge of my political duties. I might have been late to embark upon a political career. Yet, I feel happy about it, because I was thus enabled to acquire an experience of facts and deeds of which I would have been otherwise deprived and of which I may now avail myself in numerous circumstances.
Mr. Speaker, I will not delay any longer than necessary the hon. members, because I intend, during my speech, to discuss agriculture in particular, which is, with lumbering, the main industry in the county of Kamouraska. Besides, when speaking about agriculture in lower Quebec, it is logical to associate it to the lumbering industry.
It is becoming, at the outset of a new year, to a good head of family or a good company accountant, to review the developments, good or bad, that occurred during the past year, in order to be able to alter one's stand, if need be. The government's achievements, during the year, have been relatively satisfactory. I well realize, however, that it is difficult for any government to satisfy each and every citizen of this country but I am confident that the government of Canada, during this past year, have acted in no

The Address-Mr. Masse partisan fashion, that they have not attempted to serve one man, one province, one municipality or one party, but have tried to stabilize the economy of the nation as a whole.
Mr. Speaker, the year began auspiciously with the Prime Minister's trip around the world.
It is important that a country like Canada be able to communicate to such distant areas the feelings it nurses for those who cannot have the same ideas or the same mentality, but who are all filled with the same spirit of mutual co-operation, for the purpose of promoting their own interests.
I was somewhat surprised by the statements made on the other side of the house yesterday and today. If account is taken of the ten by-elections held since the last general elections, in which by-elections the Liberal party carried six seats, the Progressive Conservative party three, and the C.C.F. party one only, the statements made by some prophets are somewhat surprising and there is no doubt that the Liberal party still has the confidence of the public.
In the course of the same year, the disabled persons of Canada were fully satisfied with the attitude taken by the government of the country in its endeavours to help these less fortunate ones. Consequently, it is my opinion that the Canadian government served the country very well.
I had intended at the beginning of my remarks to speak mainly of agriculture, and I must confine myself to that subject since agriculture is the main industry in Kamour-aska county.
There is no doubt that revenues were not as large last year as they had been during the preceding four years. But our Quebec farmers do not lose hope. They are not unduly optimistic but, on the other hand, they do not lean to pessimism, which no brave soul should feel.
Weather conditions were bad from early spring to the fall; farmers had a hard time seeding their fields and taking in their crop. In certain areas the crops were very good but they were not so good in other areas, and I am afraid that in some parts of my county seed grain will be less plentiful next season.
However, as lumbering is the essential complement of agriculture in my constituency, I was glad to note the good will shown by the


right hon. the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) in connection with wooded lots. For many years, I have insisted on the establishment of wooded lots on illustration stations, particularly at the Ste. Anne de la Pocatiere experimental station, for the benefit of the farmers visiting that district. I am glad today to congratulate and thank the hon. minister for this project is being implemented.
To realize how much our forests contribute to agriculture in the lower Quebec area, one need only read publication No. 890 of the federal Department of Agriculture. This pamphlet deals with wooded lots on Ontario farms and, at page 22, it is indicated that on the 162 farms which were thoroughly investigated, production reached a total value of $516 per farm.
That is indisputable proof that lumbering plays a capital role together with agriculture in regions such as ours, where forests cover about 75 per cent of the land, only 22 per cent being suitable for cultivation.
Those experiments have been conducted in the province of Ontario with the co-operation of the federal Department of Agriculture and of the Ontario government. I hope similar experiments will be undertaken in my province to show how necessary it is to complement farming through the use of a wooded lot in most regions.
On behalf of the farmers of my county and a number of co-operative societies, namely the U.C.C., I ask the Minister of Agriculture to maintain in operation the Agricultural Prices Support Act, especially with respect to butter. The average farm in our province covers from 80 to 100 "arpents" and earned for its owner, last year, from $1,400 to $1,500. However, after the farmer has paid his municipal taxes, amounting to around $100, provided for the maintenance of his buildings, valued at some $8,000 or $10,000, and for a family of five or six children, his income is practically all spent. I therefore believe it is in the government's interest to maintain the stand it has taken regarding the support of farm prices.
Mr. Speaker, I had intended to say a few words on the problem of unemployment, but I am rather pleased with the government's stand on the matter. In the past there was no unemployment among our Quebec farmers, but today modern ideas have somewhat changed the attitude or thinking of our young
men.

I think it is time for all workers, whether they be on farms or elsewhere, to contribute to and enjoy unemployment insurance benefits in order that in circumstances which are entirely beyond their control they may be in a position to meet the situation.
I have a suggestion to make to the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mr. Pickersgill). As it happens my remarks have been misinterpreted in this house, so much so that I am believed to be opposed to immigration, which is not the case. As regards my own constituency more particularly, I believe that the available space is rather restricted. Would it not be possible to restrict immigration during the winter months, that is from November to March, taking into account the rigours of our climate and the situation with which the new Canadian is faced on his arrival? I believe that that would help to make the future home of newcomers more pleasant.

On motion of Mr. Masse the debate was adjourned.

A message was delivered by Major C. R. Lamoureux, Gentleman Usher of the Black Rod, as follows:
Mr. Speaker, the Honourable the Deputy Governor General desires the immediate attendance of this honourable house in the chamber of the honourable the Senate.
Accordingly, Mr. Speaker with the house went up to the Senate chamber.
And being returned:
The Royal Assent
Mr. Speaker informed the house that the Deputy Governor General had been pleased to give, in Her Majesty's name, the royal assent to the following bill:
An act to amend the Unemployment Insurance Act.
